name: Photos and PDFs sent to Happy are read and answered (attachment intake switched on)
description: Send a photo of a flyer, label or receipt, or a PDF packet, and Happy reads it and answers questions about it. Today a message that is only an attachment is dropped without a reply, so the first step is switching attachment intake on.
how: Set channels.imessage.includeAttachments: true; Basic mode already carries media, the default attachment root covers the happy user, and the inbound caps are 10 MB for an image and 20 MB for audio. Images then pass natively to gpt-6-sol; attached PDFs arrive as extracted text blocks; the optional pdf tool (group:media) adds page selection via local PDFium, 10 MB and 20 pages by default.
caveats: The same switch also lets voice memos and video in. Audio auto-detection tries a configured provider key before any local binary, and the documented OpenAI default for that is a cloud transcription model, so a voice memo could be sent to a cloud transcription service: set tools.media.audio.enabled: false until local transcription (F003) is in place. The docs also say attachments are still passed to the model when understanding is disabled, so check once on a live turn what a voice memo turns into. Whether the family's custom provider ids count as such a key is undocumented.

Happy cannot watch video on this provider set: the bundled video-understanding providers are Google, Qwen and Moonshot and none is configured. Add a line to AGENTS.md so Happy says so and asks for a photo or a few screenshots; a clip's sound track could later reuse the local transcription path from F003.

store:false covers less than it reads: OpenAI still keeps abuse-monitoring logs, which can include prompt and response content, for up to 30 days unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention, so family photos sent to the model fall under that.
corrections: Catalog JSON 'needs' says view_image is already granted and sets agents.defaults.pdfModel to luna. The minimal profile contains only session_status and gateway (tool-policy.md:36), and pdfModel is an agents.defaults key that is unset by default (pdf.md:124). The Markdown already drops both.
unverified: Reading accuracy on blurry phone photos and scanned image-only PDFs was not measured; pages with under 200 characters of text are rendered to images for the vision model (pdf.md:93).
Whether PDF links, as opposed to attachments, should be readable is left open; the pdf tool rejects remote URLs when it runs sandboxed (pdf.md:68).
That the gateway process under the happy account already has Full Disk Access to the Messages attachments folder comes from the 9 Oct notes and was not re-checked.
Whether OpenClaw treats the per-person custom provider ids exactly like the stock OpenAI provider for image input was not tested live (the config repo does declare image input for both models).

name: Voice memos in, transcribed locally
description: A parent sends a voice memo instead of typing; the Mac mini transcribes it locally, echoes the text back and answers. The speech-to-text step runs on the Mac mini; that the audio file itself is also kept away from the cloud model still has to be confirmed on a live turn.
how: Explicit tools.media.models CLI entry (whisper-cli, capabilities audio, {{AttachmentPath}}) plus echoTranscript; needs brew whisper.cpp, ffmpeg and a GGML model file; OpenClaw converts to WAV itself.
corrections: Markdown pairs a whisper-cpp install with audio.preferredModel: "cli:whisper". The matcher compares that value with cli: plus the entry's exact command string (dist/resolve-KJuMET3H.mjs:148), so for whisper-cpp it must be cli:whisper-cli, or cli: plus the full path used in the entry; cli:whisper only matches the Python whisper CLI.

The Homebrew formula is now named whisper.cpp (formerly whisper-cpp) and its page says GGML model files are not downloaded by default. The 9 Oct note about a model that downloads automatically describes the Python whisper CLI (media-understanding.md:168), not whisper-cli.

ffmpeg is a hard requirement the Markdown leaves out: upstream whisper-cli reads only 16-bit WAV (github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp README), OpenClaw shells out to ffmpeg for that conversion (dist/ffmpeg-exec-VIr-PIWC.mjs:25 prints the brew install hint), and the formula does not pull ffmpeg in.
unverified: The container format of iMessage voice memos, and whether ffmpeg decodes it cleanly, were not tested.
Transcription speed on the M5 Pro and accuracy for Chinese or mixed-language speech were not measured.
Whether the per-person custom provider ids count as OpenAI audio auth in auto-detection is undocumented; the explicit CLI entry sidesteps the question.

That only the transcript reaches the cloud model: the media docs say the original attachment is still passed to the model, and the model's listed inputs are text and image, so the audio file should be left out, but this was not checked on a live turn.

name: Spoken replies in a local voice (macOS say first, a neural voice later, cloud speech switched off)
description: On request, or after a voice memo, Happy's reply also arrives as an audio file to tap and play, synthesized entirely on the Mac mini: first with the built-in macOS `say` voice, which needs no install, later with a natural neural voice. Read-aloud answers, briefs and later any kids' content then never touch a cloud TTS provider, but only once the default-on Microsoft online voice is disabled in config. The same local engine can later serve Talk mode, which has its own speech setting.
example: Parent texts: read me today's brief. Or sends `/tts latest` after a long answer and gets an audio file back in iMessage.
how: Gateway `tts` block. Step 1, no install: provider `tts-local-cli` running the macOS `say` command (WAV file, offline), with `tts.auto: "inbound"` per agent so a voice memo gets a voice answer, and `/tts latest` or `/tts audio` on demand. Step 2, a natural voice, one of three documented routes. Option A: Speech Swift's local server on loopback (`brew install speech`, `speech-server --port 8080`) with the `openai` speech provider pointed at the loopback base URL, `model` tts-1 (which selects Kokoro) and `responseFormat` wav. Option B: `tts-local-cli` running the `speech` command. Option C: a Piper voice through sherpa-onnx; the bundled sherpa-onnx-tts skill runs a local binary from a shell, which needs an exec tool no agent here has, so in practice point `tts-local-cli` at that binary. In every step set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, so the default-on Microsoft online provider cannot serve as a fallback when the local engine fails. Per-agent control through `agents.entries.<id>.tts` (off for research and inbox). iMessage gets a plain audio attachment, not a voice bubble. ffmpeg on the host for conversions.
depends_on: F003 for the voice-memo round trip (tts.auto inbound)
Homebrew installs done from the admin account (speech, ffmpeg), for the neural voice only
decision: which local engine
caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.

Local-only is not the default. The keyless Microsoft provider is enabled by default, and the docs say other configured providers act as fallbacks, so a stopped local server could end in a cloud call unless Microsoft is disabled.

`/tts provider <id>` is open to any authorized sender and writes one preference file on the gateway host, so a single text can move speech to another provider for everyone. Having no cloud provider configured is the control; a prompt rule is not.

Option A adds a third-party Homebrew package and a long-running loopback server under the happy user, plus a model download: an install, a launch agent, a firewall rule and a one-time egress exception.
The loopback route needs Speech Swift v0.0.23 or later. It is a 0.0.x project, so pin the version and expect rough edges; the server also needs its own launchd job to stay up.
None of `speech`, `speech-server` or `ffmpeg` is installed on this Mac today.
iMessage outbound media is capped by `channels.imessage.mediaMaxMb` (default 16 MB), which bounds the length of a WAV reply.
In the car the phone already does the speaking: Siri announces Happy's text replies (VOX-06), so no audio file is needed there.
safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. It is local-only, and so usable for kids' content later, only after the cloud speech providers are disabled in config and blocked at the proxy; the default provider chain and the provider slash command would otherwise allow a cloud voice. Long replies pass through a summary model before synthesis, which must be local or off for kids. Keep provider switching by directive off (VOX-03).
unverified: Kokoro or Piper voice quality and speed on this Mac.
Whether pointing `tts.providers.openai` at loopback has any side effect on the earlier decision not to add a catalog openai model provider (it is a different config block).
Whether scheduled announce deliveries (briefs) pass through Auto-TTS or only interactive replies do.
Which hosts the Speech Swift package contacts to download its models.

Whether a failed local synthesis actually falls through to the Microsoft online provider when only one provider block is written. The docs say other configured providers are fallbacks and that Microsoft is enabled by default; this was not tested.
That the documented say preset writes a valid WAV on macOS 27 without extra data-format flags was not run.
How Messages on iPhone presents a WAV attachment (inline player or plain file) was not tested.
The 1,500-character summarise-or-truncate threshold is documented (tts/commands.md:104) but its effect on long replies here was not tried.

name: In the car: Siri plus iMessage, with a driving reply style
description: While driving, a parent talks to Happy through what the car already has: Siri sends the iMessage and announces Happy's reply. Happy's part is a driving style: at most two short sentences, no links, no lists, numbers written for speech, details deferred until parked.
example: Hey Siri, text Happy: driving, what time does practice end and who has pickup?
how:
No new tool or plugin. A rule in each

-main AGENTS.md: when a message starts with the word driving (or the person says they are in the car), answer in at most two plain sentences and offer to send the rest later. Siri's message announcements in CarPlay do the listening and speaking.
caveats: I found no CarPlay surface in the installed OpenClaw docs or changelog (a search for the word returned nothing), so there is no Happy app on the car screen to plan for.
The OpenClaw Start Live Voice shortcut is not a car feature: it needs the phone unlocked and the app in the foreground.
Anything that needs a tap, such as an approval prompt, has to wait until parked.
This is mostly the phone doing its job; the only work is making Happy's replies fit to be read aloud.
Announced replies are heard by everyone in the car, so the driving style should also hold back private detail (money, health, the other adult's plans) until parked.
The example needs calendar knowledge Happy does not have yet; today the rule only improves weather and search answers.

Apple's CarPlay page says that when a message is long, Siri announces only the sender's name and that a message arrived, and reads it in full only when asked. A long reply from Happy is therefore not heard unless the driver asks, which is the real reason for the two-sentence cap.
safety: Identical to typed iMessage: allowlisted sender, same agent, same hooks, same family-only outbound pin. No new device credential and no audio leaves the phone other than through Apple's own Siri.
unverified: Whether a voice memo (F003) can be recorded hands-free in CarPlay.
Apple's detailed CarPlay Messages pages returned only navigation when fetched, so only the general CarPlay support page is cited.
How long a message has to be before Siri stops reading it out, and how several messages in a row are announced.

A `before_dispatch` keyword hook that keeps a short-lived car flag on the session. The installed docs describe that hook as a claim on the inbound message, not a way to shape the reply, so the AGENTS.md rule is the mechanism to rely on.

name: Family-only delivery: text the other parent or the parents' group, and ask-and-relay a yes or no, with the recipient pinned in code
description: Happy can pass a short text from one parent to the other or to the parents' group, and can ask the other parent a question, relay the yes or no back and remind once before the ask expires. It can never message anyone outside the family.
example: Tony texts: 'Ask Jordan if she can do Thursday pickup.' Jordan gets one line, answers 'yes', and Tony gets her answer back.
how:
Delivery (G009): the `message` tool on

-main with a `before_tool_call` plugin hook that blocks any target not in family.json5 and fails closed. The live config has both `tools.message.crossContext` switches off, which confines sends to the current conversation, so `allowWithinProvider` is turned back on (`allowAcrossProviders` stays off) and the hook is then the only recipient limit. Host jobs use `openclaw agent --deliver` or `openclaw message send`. Request relay (G010), an optional second step that need not hold up the first: a pending_requests table in the household store, a `before_dispatch` plugin that matches a bare yes or no from the asked parent to that parent's one open request, and a one-shot `--at` automation for the reminder and the expiry.
caveats: Only the before_tool_call check fails closed; a message_sending hook can be added as a second check but is logged and skipped when its handler throws or times out, so it must not be relied on.
Re-opening the same-provider crossContext switch makes the hook the only recipient limit, and the hook and its family-only test case do not exist yet.
The exact parameter that carries the recipient in a message tool call, which the hook must match, was not read from source.
`openclaw message send` takes no agent flag and runs as the configured System Agent; whether that suits per-person jobs was not tested.
The relay step adds little, because the parents can already text each other or ask in the parents' group chat (F006): the gain is tracking, one reminder and an expiry.
In iMessage Basic mode there is no tap-to-answer, so the reply to a relayed request is a typed yes or no.
How plugin code sends the relayed answer on to the other parent is unverified, since no plugin-side outbound send call was found in the docs read.
For anyone outside the family (a plumber, a coach, carpool parents) Happy returns paste-ready wording and the parent sends it from their own phone.
corrections: Markdown adds message_sending 'as a second gate'. That hook can cancel a send, but when its handler throws or times out it is logged and skipped (hooks/reference.md:94), so it fails open; only the before_tool_call check is fail-closed.

The 9 Oct 'needs' implies that enabling the tool plus the hook is enough. The live config turns both crossContext switches off, and tool-permissions.md:39 says that confines sends to the current conversation, so the same-provider switch must be re-opened and the hook then becomes the only recipient limit.
unverified: The exact parameter that carries the recipient in a message tool call, which the hook must match, was not read from source.
openclaw message send takes no agent flag and runs as the configured System Agent (cli/message.md:35-50); whether that suits per-person jobs was not tested.
The hook plugin and its family-only test case do not exist yet, so blocking an unknown recipient is unproven on this install.
How plugin code sends the relayed answer to the other parent; no plugin-side outbound send call was found in the docs read, and it depends on the family delivery primitive (G009).
Group-chat use assumes iMessage groups, which are switched off today.
Judgement, not sourced: the parents can already text each other, so the gain is only tracking, expiry and the calendar offer.
safety:
This is the house rule that outbound messages go only to the family, enforced by code that fails closed and not by a prompt. It gives

-main, which holds private data, a way out limited to the two parents and their group chat. The relay step adds no new recipient and no new data source.

name: Built-in chat commands for parents (/stop, /new, /btw, /status, /usage, /tools, /loop)
description: A handful of typed commands that already work in the iMessage thread: stop an answer that is going wrong, start a clean conversation, see what Happy can do right now, and check health and cost, all handled before any model call. Two more do use the model: /btw asks a side question that is not remembered (its page does not list iMessage, so treat it as untested here), and /loop (owner only, and only once the scheduling tool is granted in F007) starts a repeating check inside a thread.
example: Jordan texts '/stop' when a long answer is heading the wrong way, then '/new'. Tony texts '/loop 30m tell me when the winter storm warning ends'.
how:
Text commands are core and work on iMessage: command-only messages from allowlisted senders are handled before the queue and the model. /stop aborts the active run in that chat; /new archives the session and starts fresh; /tools lists the agent's effective tools; /status shows runtime, uptime and plugin health; /usage tokens|full|cost toggles a per-reply footer or prints a cost summary. /btw answers from the current session with a separate one-shot model query and writes nothing to history. /loop is owner-only and asks the agent to create a recurring agent-turn job bound to the conversation through the cron (automations) tool, at a fixed interval or self-paced between one minute and one hour, so it works only after F007 grants that tool to

-main. Put the five everyday ones in templates/person/AGENTS.md and a one-screen cheat sheet. The config-writing commands stay off as today, and Tony should decide whether /restart, which is on by default for owners, stays available from chat.
depends_on: G005 kill switch for the stop-everything case

F007 (automations/cron tool on

-main) before /loop works at all; Jordan in the owner list if she should use it
caveats: /stop ends one run in one chat; it does not pause scheduled jobs, so it complements the G005 kill phrase rather than replacing it.

/loop needs owner status, which only Tony has today, and it asks the agent to create the job with the cron (automations) tool, so it does nothing until

-main holds that tool (F007).
The /btw page names WhatsApp, Telegram and Discord for channel use and does not mention iMessage.
/usage figures are local estimates, like G004.
In a plain iMessage bubble the /status and /tools output may be long.

A /loop job is written by the model in chat, outside the G003 jobs registry, and is capped to the tools of the turn that created it; a self-paced loop may run as often as once a minute, so count it under G004 and review it with /loop status.

name: Research agent: reads public web pages behind egress guardrails, with cited answers and background-task etiquette
description: Happy can read public web pages that load without JavaScript or a login: a memory-less research helper fetches the page and the parent's own agent relays the answer with its link and the time it was fetched. Slow lookups get an 'on it', one message when done and a working 'cancel that', and nothing the helper fetches can reach the home network.
example: Jordan texts: 'What time does the town pool open on Saturday? Check their site.' Happy replies 'on it', then sends the hours with the link and when the page was fetched.
how:
Agent (F019): a new `research` agent, memory search off, tools `web_search` and `web_fetch`, sandboxed; each

-main gains `sessions_spawn` and `subagents.allowAgents: ["research"]`; its rules live in AGENTS.md only. Guardrails (WEB-01): leave both `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` keys unset, keep `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, install no fetch-provider plugin, set `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`, keep `browser.enabled: false` until F020, and add two eval cases (a LAN address, a public URL that redirects to one) to the M3 exit test. Answer rules (F022): quote `fetchedAt`, use `published` when present, flag pages undated or older than 30 days, allow 'could not verify'; a fact check returns true, false, mixed or unclear with two or three dated sources. Etiquette (G014): `runTimeoutSeconds` on the spawn, the automatic completion announce, `subagents` `action: "cancel"`, and concurrency caps.
caveats: The plain fetch runs no JavaScript and cannot log in, so such pages wait for the research browser (F020) or stay unread.

web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects, but the browser's own check is weaker (the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall), which matters once F020 switches the browser on.

Leave the private-network keys truly unset: an explicitly written `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` turns hostname navigation into an allowlist and would stop a later research browser from loading hostnames.

The SSRF policy covers the `web_fetch` and browser tools only, so host-side helpers that take a URL (the summarize wrapper, the print plugin's download, watcher scripts) need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks.

A hostname block list is not an exfiltration control and is not worth curating: what counts is the private-network block, no headers, no fallback provider, and no private data in the agent that browses.

Once research has web_fetch, the roadmap's egress proxy cannot double as an exfiltration allowlist; it can deny private ranges and named hosts and nothing more (an inference from the routing description).
A sandboxed requester cannot spawn an unsandboxed target, so research has to stay sandboxed, and sub-agents keep only AGENTS.md, so every citation and no-login rule must be in that one file.
An official-sites-only mode for admin questions would need a before_tool_call hook and is not planned.
corrections: The 9 Oct verifier notes advised turning the sandbox off for research; the installed docs say a sandboxed requester cannot spawn an unsandboxed target, so the catalog's final wording (keep mode all) is the only workable one.
A verifier note asked for research rules in AGENTS.md and SOUL.md; the installed docs say sub-agents keep only AGENTS.md, so every citation and no-login rule must be in that one file.
unverified: That a cross-agent handoff returns its result with agent-to-agent messaging off: the roadmap lists this as untested on 2026.9.7 and the CLI was not run here.

The handoff privacy rule (ages yes, names and school no) is a prompt rule; nothing mechanical enforces what

-main writes into the task text.
The roadmap's plan to drop LAN access inside the Colima VM would not cover a browser that runs on the host; this follows from where the process runs and was not tested.
Which hosts belong on the blocklist is a judgment call, not something the docs prescribe.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.
Nothing in the installed stack enforces citations; this is a prompt rule the model can ignore, and Tony's promptfoo evals are the only check.
The 30-day staleness threshold and the three-links-per-text cap are house choices with no source.
Nothing on the current stack runs longer than about 20 seconds, so the convention has no user until the research hand-off (F019) exists.
The acknowledgement wording and the 'about three minutes' estimate are prompt conventions; the model can skip them.
safety: The research agent reads untrusted pages but holds no memory, no accounts and no family data, and the guardrails take the home network out of its reach; that is what breaks the trifecta. They do not stop an injected page making it request some public URL. Its answer returns to an agent that holds memory, so the relayed text is treated as untrusted.

name: Family facts, standing preferences and reply language rendered into each parent's agent from family.json5
description: Both parents' agents start every chat already knowing the kids' school, routines and activities and each adult's standing preferences, including the language to reply in. On request Happy also turns a school note into a short Chinese text a parent can forward to a grandparent.
example: Jordan writes to Happy in Chinese and is answered in Chinese; Tony texts 'put this school note in Chinese for grandma' and gets three short lines to forward.
how: One generator, one file. From family.json5 the generator renders each adult's directives into USER.md (4,000-character cap), the per-person reply-language line among them (G011), and the kid and routine facts into MEMORY.md with trigger comments (F042); nothing is rendered into shared agents. Scheduled jobs do not read that line, so the language is written into each job message. The grandparent version is a prompt-only request on the parent's own agent: no new tool and no send path, and the parent forwards the text.
caveats: USER.md has a 4,000-character cap that all standing preferences share, so the list has to stay short.

Rendered facts change only when the family file is edited and redeployed, and a chat edit to a generated file is expected to be lost on the next deploy; things a parent says in chat go through the memory write path (F041).

On supported iPhones Messages can already translate a conversation automatically and on device, so plain back-and-forth with a grandparent may need nothing from Happy; whether that covers Chinese on this family's phones is not confirmed.
Happy's distinct part on the language side is the shortened Chinese version of a school note, and its translation quality for school notices was not evaluated.

A per-language voice switch is documented only for the bundled Microsoft speech provider, which is an online service, so it does not help the offline say path, and whether the default say voice pronounces Chinese was not tested.
The generator script and the family registry were not opened in this review.
corrections: A 9 Oct verifier note says there is no per-language voice switch. tts/output.md:56 documents one for the bundled Microsoft provider, which is an online service; it does not help the offline say path.
unverified: The generator script and the family registry live in happy-config and were not opened in this run.
That a chat edit to a generated file is lost on the next deploy is a property of Tony's generator, not something an opened source states.
Translation quality into Chinese by gpt-6-sol for school notices was not evaluated.
Which iPhone models and languages Apple's Live Translation covers for this family was not confirmed; the Apple page defers to an availability list.
Whether the macOS say default voice pronounces Chinese text was not tested.
safety: The rendered files hold the children's school and routines, so they go only into the two parents' own agents and never into shared agents such as research, the group agent or the mail readers. No tool and no send path are added; a translated note leaves the family only when a parent forwards it.

description: One shared family handbook that both parents' agents can search: people, home systems, providers, renewal dates, sitter notes. Registry (F034): with inbound attachments on, the vision model reads the data plate and the agent saves a wiki synthesis page with `wiki_apply`, or a fact in the household store; manuals given as a link go through the research agent. Data-plate photos go to the cloud vision model, which is the attachments decision recorded under F002, and image input on the family's custom provider ids was not re-checked.
The vault is shared by design, so both parents' agents search and edit the same pages.

name: Teach Happy a routine (operator-reviewed skills)
description: A parent describes once how the family does something; it becomes a named skill Happy follows every time (party plan, ski-trip packing, school-form explainer). A skill goes live only after Tony has read it.
example: Happy, learn our ski-trip packing routine: ask how many nights and who is coming, then list by person, and always include the kids' helmets.
how:
Happy answers with the drafted procedure as plain text (no tool needed). Tony turns it into `skills//SKILL.md` (a `name` and a one-line `description`, optionally `user-invocable`) in happy-config under that person's template, reviews it, and happy-deploy copies it into that agent's workspace `skills/` folder, the highest-precedence skill root. To use a skill the model must load its SKILL.md with the `read` tool; the system prompt lists only each skill's name, description and location. So

-main needs `read` in `tools.alsoAllow` and in the sandbox tool allowlist (group:fs is denied today). With `workspaceAccess: "none"` OpenClaw mirrors eligible skills into the sandbox workspace as read-only copies and `read` is rooted there. Keep `skill_workshop` denied on every family agent. Alternative for agent-scoped Workshop skills: `openclaw skills workshop propose-create --agent

-main --proposal ./PROPOSAL.md`, then inspect and apply, run as the happy user from the deploy path. Per-agent visibility through `agents.entries..skills`; inbox keeps `skills: []`. Held by the asking parent's

-main; shared stateless agents get only skills meant for everyone. A routine of a few lines can instead live as a section of AGENTS.md, which needs no tool.
depends_on: a skills step in happy-deploy and gen-family
automatic self-learning switched off in config (`skills.workshop.autonomous.mode: "off"`)
decision: who may request a new skill

`read` allowed on

-main in tools.alsoAllow and the sandbox tool allowlist (group:fs is denied today; arrives with F041)
caveats: Asking Happy to save a skill from iMessage does not work on this stack by default: sandboxed runs do not construct the `skill_workshop` tool even when it is allowlisted, so `/learn` cannot stage a draft. The M1 doctor baseline in the config repo already shows this warning for every agent. The documented exception is a human turn with host-granted library-authoring authority, and personal-library authoring publishes with no pending draft, which would skip Tony's review. That is one more reason to keep `skill_workshop` off every family agent's allowlist.
A skill is know-how. It cannot add tools or accounts, so "learn to order the groceries" still ends at a list.
A skill is instruction text loaded into future sessions. One written from a pasted web page or an email is a stored injection, so author only from the parent's own words.
No marketplace skills: an audit reported by The Hacker News found 341 malicious entries among 2,857 ClawHub skills in early 2026.
Turnaround is "when Tony next deploys", not instant.
A new or changed workspace skill is picked up on the next turn after the skills watcher sees the file change, or after the gateway restart that a deploy performs. No /new is needed.
safety:
Operator review is the gate: no model-written file ever reaches a skills root. A skill cannot widen tool policy, so the trifecta split between

-main, research and the mail readers is unchanged. Per-person skills live in that person's workspace, so nothing crosses data domains.
unverified: Whether a user-invocable skill command typed by an allowlisted non-owner iMessage sender is accepted on 2026.9.7.
That skill sync into the sandbox works with `workspaceAccess: "none"` (the docs say sandboxed runs read materialized copies).

That a `read`-only grant on a sandboxed

-main reaches the mirrored skills and nothing private; check at build time.
Whether an iMessage owner turn is ever given library-authoring authority on this configuration. If it is, an allowlisted `skill_workshop` could publish a skill with no review.

name: More read-only Google data per person: Sheets, Docs, Drive and Contacts
description: An adult can ask about a named Google Sheet or Doc (chore chart, house projects) and get the answer read from the file where it already lives, or ask for a person's or a vendor's number from their own Google Contacts. Nothing is changed or moved.
example: Jordan texts: 'What is next on the house projects sheet?' or 'What is the plumber's number?'
how: Both ride on the gog command-line tool and each adult's own Google sign-in, the same sign-in step as the calendar and Gmail readers. Sheets, Docs and Drive (F045): register `gog mcp` with `openclaw mcp add`; write tools stay hidden by default, `--allow-tool drive_search,drive_get,docs_get,sheets_read_range` narrows it further, and it is allowed only on that person's main. Contacts (G013): gog's MCP server lists no Contacts tool, so a thin read-only stdio MCP wrapper around gog's contacts listing is still needed, registered per person in the same way with the contacts service consented.
caveats: gog is not installed, so which version ships `gog mcp`, its contacts subcommands and the scopes it requests were not checked locally, and no first-party page opened shows a read-only Drive scope choice at consent time.
Whether the family keeps anything useful in Sheets is unknown.
Only Google Contacts is covered, because an Apple Contacts route was never sourced.
A Drive search can return files that other people have shared with the account, so what Happy reads there may be untrusted text.
With sandbox mode all, MCP tools also have to be named in the sandbox tool gate, as for the Gmail and calendar readers.
The contacts lookup mainly serves sitter sheets and paste-ready vendor drafts that need the right number.
corrections:
The catalog plans a custom `

-drive-ro` wrapper because gog was taken to be CLI-only. gogcli.sh/mcp documents `gog mcp`, a typed stdio MCP server exposing drive_search, drive_get, docs_get and sheets_read_range, so this feature needs no custom wrapper.

The 9 Oct note says no read-only option is documented for gog. The same upstream page documents that write tools stay hidden unless --allow-write is passed and that a read-only policy cannot be widened by it, and the gog README shows a global --readonly flag; the bundled skill file simply does not mention them.

The 9 Oct note says gog is a CLI and not an MCP server. gogcli.sh/mcp documents `gog mcp`, a stdio MCP server; its listed tools include no Contacts tool, so the planned contacts wrapper is still needed.
unverified: gog is not installed, so which version ships `gog mcp` and which OAuth scopes it requests for Drive and Sheets were not checked locally; no first-party page opened here shows a read-only Drive scope choice at consent time.
Whether the family keeps anything useful in Sheets is unknown.
gog is not installed on the Mac, so its version, its contacts subcommands and the exact scope it requests were not checked locally.
The Apple Contacts through a Shortcut alternative was not sourced in this cluster.
safety: Read-only on that adult's own account, but it lands on the agent that holds the adult's memory. A Drive search can surface files shared by other people, which is untrusted text, so keep the lookup to files the adult owns or names and decide before building whether shared files are read at all. Contacts stay on their owner's agent.

name: Per-person mail agent with read-only Gmail: 'did I get an email about X?'
description: One locked-down mail agent per adult can search and read that adult's own Gmail under a read-only grant: nothing is changed, labelled or sent, and the agent cannot browse, run code or message anyone but its owner. A parent asks 'did the dentist confirm?' and gets the sender, the date and the gist, or a five-line timeline of the thread.
example: Tony texts: 'Did the dentist confirm Thursday?' Happy answers with the sender, the date and one line of gist from his own inbox.
how:
Agent (G015): one `

-mail` entry per adult with `profile: "minimal"`, an explicit `

-gmail__*` allow plus the `tools.sandbox.tools` gate, web, fs, runtime and browser denied, memory search off for that agent, and an owner-pinned send hook for its own scheduled turns; checked with `openclaw sandbox explain --agent`. Tool (F047): `gog mcp` as a host-side stdio entry under `mcp.servers`, read tools only, one token per adult, authorised with `--gmail-scope readonly`. Hand-off:

-main spawns

-mail through `subagents.allowAgents` and gets a bounded answer back. Scheduled sweeps of named senders would use this same read-only tool; the IMAP watch on a personal inbox was dropped.
caveats: The roadmap's M4 keeps each inbox on a local model and none is installed, so this sends personal mail to the cloud model, and without Zero Data Retention the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to that text.
gog is not installed on this Mac, so its flags come from upstream docs and must be confirmed with `gog mcp --list-tools` and `gog auth add --help` on the installed version.
With sandbox mode all, MCP tools stay hidden unless `tools.sandbox.tools` names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob, and the minimal profile does not allow MCP tools implicitly.
'Memory off' is not one switch: memory search has a per-agent override, dreaming is plugin-wide, and the session-exclusion setting only matches hook sessions.

'Send pinned to owner' applies only when the mail agent runs its own scheduled or hook turn, because a mail agent spawned from

-main always loses `message` and `session_status`.

Whether both adults' tokens would share one keyring under the happy user is open (a per-adult GOG_HOME is an inference), and the refresh-token lifetime of a self-made Google OAuth client left in testing status was not checked.
That a before_tool_call hook reaches MCP tool calls is implied by the docs, but no sentence there names MCP tools.
The thread-summary half is free inside Gmail now, so what this adds is asking from the iMessage thread.
corrections: The 9 Oct needs list omits the sandbox-layer gate: with sandbox mode 'all', MCP tools stay hidden unless `tools.sandbox.tools` names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130). The minimal profile does not allow MCP tools implicitly either (same file, lines 36 and 41).

'Memory off' is not one switch in the installed docs: memory search has a per-agent override (`agents.entries.*.memory.search`, `enabled`, docs/reference/memory-config.md:31 and :102), dreaming is plugin-wide (docs/concepts/memory.md:275), and `excludeSessions.hookExternalContentSources` only matches hook sessions (docs/reference/memory-config.md:667).

'Send pinned to owner' only applies when the mail agent runs its own scheduled or hook turn: when spawned from `

-main` it always loses `message` and `session_status` (docs/tools/subagents/tool-policy.md:23), so its allow list must not consist of `session_status` alone.
The 9 Oct needs list puts `openclaw models status --agent --probe` in the deploy checks; the installed doc says a direct probe needs the Gateway stopped (docs/cli/models.md:121).

The 9 Oct verifier note says gogcli has no read-only-only Gmail scope. The upstream command reference lists `--gmail-scope full|readonly|send|read-send` and says `--readonly` on `gog auth add` requests read-only OAuth scopes, so a read-only grant can be requested; the catalog's hedge 'if the installed version supports it' can be firmed up, pending a check on the installed binary.

The 9 Oct text treats the `

-gmail` wrapper as new code. Upstream gogcli ships a stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`) that exposes only read tools unless `--allow-write` is passed, so the config entry can run gog directly with an `--allow-tool` list and no wrapper.

The 9 Oct needs list stops at the per-agent allow list. With sandbox mode 'all' (Happy's setting) the installed docs add a second gate: MCP tools are filtered out unless `tools.sandbox.tools` also names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130).
unverified: The per-person provider setting that sends store false was verified in M1 and not re-read here.
Whether this OpenAI account has zero retention; without it the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to mail text sent to the model.
The promptfoo boundary canary is in-house.
A before_tool_call hook reaching MCP tool calls is implied by the doc ('every tool call in the run', docs/plugins/hooks/tool-policy.md:222) but I found no sentence naming MCP tools.
gog is not installed on this Mac; the flags come from the upstream main-branch docs and must be confirmed with `gog mcp --list-tools` and `gog auth add --help` on the version Homebrew installs.

Whether both adults' tokens would sit in one keyring under the happy user: upstream says tokens use the platform keyring by default with a file backend for headless hosts; splitting them with a per-adult GOG_HOME is my inference from the paths doc.
Refresh-token lifetime for a self-made Google OAuth client left in testing status was not checked in this run; Google's scope page does mark gmail.readonly as a Restricted scope.
The promptfoo injection canary is an in-house test, not an OpenClaw feature.
safety: The mail agent holds private mail and reads untrusted mail text, so it gets no way out: no web, files, runtime or browser, and messages only to its owner. Read-only means Google's read-only scope on a per-adult token. Draft writing and sending are separate cards with their own grants, so no write path is hidden here.

name: Drafts in the owner's Gmail Drafts (Happy drafts, the owner sends)
description: A parent asks by text for a reply or a note, and Happy leaves it as a draft in that parent's own Gmail Drafts, threaded under the mail it answers. The parent reviews and sends from Gmail; sending is switched off for Happy.
example: Tony texts: 'Reply to the plumber: Tuesday after 3 works.' A threaded draft is waiting in his Gmail Drafts.
how: One drafts server per adult with its own token: `gog --gmail-no-send mcp --allow-write --allow-tool gmail_create_draft,gmail_update_draft`, callable only by that adult's own agents. gog registers its send tools only with a separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag, which is never passed; a fail-closed `before_tool_call` hook that blocks any send tool is the second layer. For threading the CLI has `gog gmail drafts reply <messageId>` and `--reply-to-message-id` on `drafts create`.
caveats: Gmail itself now drafts replies for free (Help Me Write and Suggested Replies), inside the thread a parent has to open anyway to press send. Happy's version helps when the request starts in iMessage or needs family facts Happy already holds, so it ranks below the school mailbox.
Google offers no drafts-only permission: the sign-in that can write drafts could also send. What stops sending is gog's no-send switch and the hook, not Google.
corrections: The catalog says 'verify `--reply-to-message-id` on drafts create, else drafts are unthreaded'. The upstream command reference documents `--reply-to-message-id` and `--thread-id` on `gog gmail drafts create`, plus a separate `gog gmail drafts reply <messageId>`; the installed SKILL.md (line 59) merely omits them.

The catalog describes a custom MCP around `gog gmail drafts create` with the hook as the only send barrier. Upstream gog's own MCP server already keeps `gmail_send_message` and `gmail_send_draft` behind a separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag, so the hook is a second layer, not the only one.
unverified: Whether gog's MCP tool `gmail_create_draft` exposes the reply and thread parameters that the CLI command has; if not, threaded drafts need a thin wrapper over the CLI.
gog is not installed here; confirm the tool names with `gog mcp --allow-write --list-tools` after install.
The promptfoo 'send attempt is blocked' test is in-house.

name: mailout: email the owner only ('email me this')
description: 'Email me this': long answers, tables and plans land in the asker's own inbox from a dedicated family sender; nobody else can be a recipient.
how:
A send-only mail tool on a dedicated family sender account: the gog MCP server with the write flag plus its separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag and only the send tool allowed, granted to `

-main` only. A `before_tool_call` hook blocks the call unless the recipient equals the owner address of the calling agent and cc and bcc are empty; a block is terminal and the hook fails closed. Do not rely on rewriting the recipient: the docs describe rewrites for host-owned tool parameters only. An in-house daily send cap.
unverified: That the hook sees every recipient field (to, cc, bcc) of the gog MCP send tool in its parameters; prove it with a seeded send to a non-owner address, which must be blocked.
A daily send cap is in-house code; no built-in cap was found in the pages read.
Creating the dedicated family sender account and granting its send scope is a manual step outside OpenClaw.

name: Kids agent (waits for a local model): own handle, homework hints, chat hours, parent alerts and a nightly digest
description: Later, each child texts Happy from their own Apple account and gets a helper with no tools and no memory, on a local model, that gives grade-level hints and short explanations and never a finished worksheet. The parents get set chat hours per child, an immediate text when a message is flagged for safety or distress, and an evening digest of what each child asked.
example: Trigger: at 21:40 the 8-year-old texts the kids agent and gets a fixed 'time for bed, ask me tomorrow' line. Separately, a message classified as distress sends both parents: 'Safety flag in the 10-year-old's chat at 16:12, please check in.'
how: Base (F072): `bindings[]` by DM handle to one agent per kid, the minimal profile with `session_status` and `gateway` denied, memory search off, a daily reset, and an in-house kid-safety plugin running a local classifier on `before_dispatch` and `message_sending`. Hints (F073): hint-first rules and a grade band in the kid agent's AGENTS.md; replies carry no URLs. Hours and alerts (MKT-13), same plugin: `before_dispatch` claims messages outside each kid's hours from family.json5 with a fixed reply and no model call; on a distress or safety label it sends a pre-written supportive reply and texts both parents the category and time through family delivery. Digest (G019): a host-side command job reads the kid agent's session history and summarises it on a local model, delivered straight to the parents.
caveats: Blocked until a local model and local classifiers exist and the kid-safety evals pass, because kids' content never goes to a cloud model or cloud speech.

A local classifier's accuracy on how 8 and 10-year-olds actually write is unproven: false alarms will annoy, misses matter more, and a home system has no human reviewer between the flag and the parent notice.
Even Google's supervised version for under-13s tells parents its filters are not perfect, so the parent alerts and the review of flagged chats are part of the base and not extras.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule, and no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
The alert is a heads-up to parents and not a crisis service, and the parents should be told so.
The chat-hours half needs no model and can ship the day the kid agent does; the safety flag and the digest need the local model.
Whether kids admitted by pairing are refused as approvers is untested, and how a plugin sends a proactive message to the parents from inside a hook was not found in the hook docs read.
Until then a parent can run a practice quiz from their own chat (MKT-02), which is the parent using the cloud model and not the child.
corrections: 'OpenAI terms are 13+, no cloud shortcut' could not be confirmed as worded: OpenAI's consumer Terms of Use returned HTTP 403 in this run, and the API page that did open sets no flat 13+ bar. It says personal data of children under 13 must not be processed without zero data retention and that COPPA applies. Keeping kids off the cloud stays the family's rule; store:false was not shown to count as zero data retention.
unverified: Llama Guard 3 as the classifier is the roadmap's choice and appears nowhere in the installed OpenClaw docs (its Ollama library page is cited under G019).
Whether kids admitted by pairing are refused as approvers; the roadmap itself marks this as untested.
How accurate any local classifier is on questions from 8 and 10 year olds; no evaluation exists yet.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule; no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
A parent asking the same questions from their own chat works today, but that is the parent using the cloud model, not the child.
Whether the Apple on-device model can be called from a host job for an ad hoc summary; the doc gives it an 8,192-token window and 1,024 output tokens and describes utility use only.
Reading the per-agent database from a command job (read-only open or the history RPC) was not tried.

Which session transcript a delivered digest line is copied into: the installed source appends direct scheduled deliveries to a session transcript (dist/delivery-dispatch-awareness-CcGkYFaV.mjs:518), and if that session belongs to a parent's cloud-backed agent, the quoted kid text would reach a cloud model.
Whether ChatGPT's controls changed after the September 2025 launch report; OpenAI's own page returned 403 in this run.
How the plugin sends a proactive message to the parents from inside a hook; G009 covers the agent `message` tool and host jobs, and no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read.
safety: No cloud call touches kid content: the agent, its classifiers and the digest summariser are local, and with the classifier down the agent answers 'ask a grown-up'. Alerts carry a category, not the child's words, and go only to the two parents. The digest quotes a child, so a host job delivers it, never into a session a cloud model later reads.

name: Scheduled-jobs registry in family.json5: per-person switches, a charter per job, failure guardrails
description: Every scheduled feature becomes a named switch per person in one reviewed file. From that entry the generator creates the job with a time limit and a tool cap and writes a short charter the parents can read: what Happy may do without asking, what needs a yes first, when to stop and ask, what it must never do. Failures alert Tony, not the family; a job that keeps failing stops itself; runs missed during a power cut are skipped.
example: Turning Jordan's school digest off is a one-line change Tony reviews. The 19:30 brief fails twice in a row: Tony gets one text, and one more when it recovers. After a power cut the 07:00 brief does not turn up at 11:40.
how: gen-family reads the family.json5 flags and emits `openclaw automations add/edit/remove`, keyed on the stable `--name`, with `--agent`, `--to`, `--tz`, `--announce`, `--timeout-seconds` and an explicit `--tools` cap on every job; it diffs against `automations list --all --json`, because the default list hides disabled jobs. The same entries render one `## Program: <name>` section per job (Authority, Trigger, Approval gate, Escalation, What NOT to do, plus an execute-verify-report rule) into templates/person/AGENTS.md, and each job message points at its program instead of repeating it; isolated jobs must not use `--light-context`, which drops the bootstrap files. Gateway config: a global `cron.failureAlert` object routed to the operator's handle; `cron.skipMissedJobs: true`; `cron.triggers.enabled: false`. These three switches are plain config and can go in before the generator exists; triggers must be off before timed reminders (F007) or any other item gives an agent the `automations` tool. happy-inspect reads `automations list --all` to catch auto-disabled jobs. The healthchecks dead-man switch stays the only signal for a Mac that is off.
caveats: A charter is prompt text, not enforcement; the hard limits stay in tool policy and hooks.

AGENTS.md shares a bootstrap budget (20,000 characters per file by default); keep each program to about ten lines. Scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md, so anything a program needs must be in AGENTS.md, the job message or a tool result.
A chat instruction does not change a charter; it waits for a reviewed deploy.
By default a failure alert goes to the failing job's own announce target, so Jordan would get 'job failed' texts for her jobs unless they are rerouted to Tony.
Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list.
Without a per-job timeout an isolated agent job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog.
After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts. One-shot reminders still catch up after an outage even with skipMissedJobs set.

Jobs an agent creates in chat, once

-main holds the automations tool, are outside the registry, so the diff must tolerate or report them.

With triggers on, trigger scripts and script payloads run with the owning agent's full tool policy, exec included. Switching triggers off also switches off the trigger-script design of F029 until that is deliberately turned back on.
corrections: Diffing against 'automations list --json' is not enough: the list shows enabled jobs only unless --all is passed, so a job disabled by a mute would look missing and be created twice. Use 'automations list --all --json'.
unverified: Whether gen-family, run from Tony's admin account, can reach the happy user's Gateway with the admin operator scope the docs require.
Whether scheduler-sent failure alerts pass through the G009 recipient-pin hook or bypass it.
Where the auto-disable notice lands: the docs say the owning agent receives it even when failure alerts are off, so it may reach the family member's thread instead of Tony's.
safety: Purely restrictive. Charters narrow behaviour and grant nothing; never-list items are written under What NOT to do and are also unreachable by tool policy. Alert text shown in chat is a normalized cause, and routing alerts to the operator keeps one person's job details out of another person's thread.

name: Stop by text: 'Happy, stop everything', and lock one person out
description: Either parent can text one exact phrase and Happy stops: no agent runs, no tool calls and no scheduled texts until Tony switches it back on at the Mac. A second phrase stops Happy answering one person's handle, for a lost or stolen phone.
example: Jordan texts 'Happy, stop everything' when briefs start arriving twice. Tony texts 'Happy, lock out Jordan' after her phone is left in a taxi.
how: In-house plugin. before_dispatch claims the exact phrase from an adult's handle and writes a kill file (everything) or a suspended file (one person's handles). The stop is enforced where hooks fail closed: before_agent_run blocks agent runs before the model reads the prompt, and before_tool_call blocks tools; message_sending cancels scheduled announce texts as a best-effort extra. Levels that need no plugin code, done by Tony: `cron.enabled: false`, then `openclaw gateway stop`. Lifting a stop or a lock-out is CLI-only. For a stolen phone the operator step still has to follow: remove the handle from family.json5 and redeploy, which is the only thing that ends that handle's approver rights; `openclaw devices revoke` if the phone ran the OpenClaw app; Find My Lost Mode on the phone side.
caveats: The phrase matcher is a claim hook and message_sending is a delivery hook: both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so the stop must not live only there.
Command jobs make no agent run, so their announce texts can only be caught by message_sending (as read from the bundled code, not yet tested); the dependable stop for those is the scheduler switch.
/stop (OCL-06) ends one answer in one chat; this stops everything.
For a stolen phone, 'stop everything' already works as the blunt version; the lock-out phrase only keeps Happy answering the other parent in the meantime.
A locked phone already stops most misuse. The lock-out covers a phone taken while unlocked or a passcode seen over a shoulder.
Either adult can lock the other out, and Tony undoes it at the Mac. If whoever holds the phone sends the phrase first, the real owner needs the CLI.
A lock-out stops replies and texts to that person, not their scheduled jobs; pause those too (G002).
Keep both phrases out of Happy's own help text and replies.
corrections: 'Freeze every outbound write' is fail-closed only for tool calls. The phrase matcher and the message_sending check both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so a broken plugin lets the phrase reach the model and lets scheduled announce texts out. The levels that do not depend on plugin code are the scheduler switch and stopping the Gateway.
unverified: That before_agent_run fires for scheduled agent-turn jobs on this build; test with a throwaway job.
Whether switching the scheduler off stops a job already running, and whether switching it back needs a restart (the hot-reload table says no; the automation troubleshooting page says restart).
How plugin code running as the happy user would change the scheduler setting, given the config repo is read-only to it; the kill file may be the only chat-triggered level.
What the sender sees when before_agent_run blocks a run and no replacement message is set.
Whether a tapback from a suspended handle can still resolve a pending approval, and whether owner-only slash commands from that handle are parsed before the plugin's hooks run.

The Shortcut and ntfy-button triggers from the 9 Oct entry: where an ntfy action request originates, and whether it can reach the Gateway over Tailscale, was not confirmed, so the text phrase is the only confirmed trigger.
safety: Both phrases can only narrow what Happy does; nothing in the chat path can add a sender or switch anything back on. A chat lock-out leaves the handle on channels.imessage.allowFrom, which is also the approver list, so that person's agent runs and tool calls must be blocked by the fail-closed hooks until Tony removes the handle and redeploys.

name: When the model is down: an honest failure, a same-vendor fallback, and jobs that need no model
description: With one cloud vendor and no local model, a provider incident makes Happy answer with a raw error or not at all. This sets what the family sees and what keeps working: one plain 'the model is down' line, an optional sibling-model fallback, and the alerts that never needed a model.
example: Trigger: gpt-6-sol returns server errors for ten minutes at 07:00 while the morning brief is due.
how:
Fact on this install: each person agent is generated with model.fallbacks: [], and the docs say an agent's primary is strict unless its model object lists fallbacks. So after the built-in retries any failure is surfaced as a terminal error that keeps the provider's HTTP status. Options, cheapest first. (1) Add gpt-6-luna on the same per-person provider id as the single fallback for

-main: one line in gen-family, since both models are already in that agent's modelPolicy.allow under the same key and store setting. This covers model-scoped incidents and rate limits, not a vendor-wide outage. The docs say a fallback is used for that turn only and a one-line notice is shown in direct chats. Mail and kid agents keep fallbacks: [] as the roadmap requires. (2) No cross-vendor fallback: it needs a second vendor's key and a new privacy decision, and the local route is the skipped M2. (3) Keep the important alerts model-free: the weather watch (F018) is specified as a --command-argv job and the kill phrase (G005) is a before_dispatch claim, so both work through an outage. Timed reminders (F007) and the morning brief are '--message' jobs, which the docs define as model-backed agent turns, so they fail with the model; a fixed-text reminder that must not be missed, such as bin day, has to be created as a command job that prints its line. A scheduled agent turn can also carry its own '--fallbacks' list. (4) Extend the health watch (G008): when the existing error-ratio alert has fired for N minutes, a host script sends each parent one fixed line and later one 'back' line by a model-free send: 'openclaw message send' to the pinned family handles, or a command job with announce delivery. The catalog's usual host path, 'openclaw agent --deliver', runs an agent turn and so cannot announce a model outage. 'openclaw models status --check' is not the detector: its own docs say a clean exit does not prove a request will succeed.
depends_on: decision: let the smaller sibling model answer when the main one fails
G008 health watch and the O1 error-ratio alert
G009 family delivery (for the notice)
caveats: OpenAI's status history listed 39 incidents in September 2026 and 23 in the first ten days of October across all its products. Most do not touch the API models Happy uses, but some did, for example 'elevated error rates across API models' on 17 Sep.
An answer from the smaller model can be worse than the usual one; the fallback notice tells the parent which model answered.
An API key that hits its monthly cap looks like an outage until the month ends; the fixed line should say 'limit reached' when that is the cause.
If the Mac, the home internet or iMessage is what failed, nothing here helps. The dead-man alert is then the only signal and it goes to Tony.
A scheduled brief that fails is simply missed unless the job's retry settings say otherwise.
safety: No new data path. The fallback uses the same provider id, key and store:false setting, and the notice is a fixed string to pinned family recipients. Mail and kid agents stay strict, so their content can never move to another model by accident.
unverified: The exact text a parent sees on iMessage when every candidate fails; the docs describe it, it was not triggered in this run.
Whether gpt-6-luna stays healthy during typical gpt-6-sol incidents.
Whether command jobs deliver normally while model calls are failing; nothing suggests otherwise but it was not tested.
Whether 'openclaw message send' passes through the same recipient-pinning hook as the agent's message tool; if it does not, the host script must hard-code the family handles from the registry.

name: Notification policy: daily cap, quiet hours, priority classes and job tags, plus snooze, mute and vacation mode by chat
description: Caps how many unprompted texts each parent gets in a day, holds non-urgent ones outside allowed hours and labels each one so you know which job sent it. Either parent can text 'mute until 3' or 'we are away next week', and briefs, bin reminders and routines pause for that window while urgent alerts still arrive.
example: Jordan texts: 'We are away next week.' Briefs and bin reminders stop for the week; an urgent alert still arrives.
how: Policy (G001): an in-house plugin with `before_tool_call` on `message` (fails closed) and a `message_sending` cancel for `--announce` deliveries (fails open on error); counters live in the household store, and schedules are generated inside the allowed windows in the first place. Pause (G002): a paused-until row in the same store that each job reads first, answering `NO_REPLY`; or `openclaw automations disable|enable <job-id>` from a host helper; `cron.enabled: false` pauses everything. The policy's priority classes decide which alerts still pass during a mute. A sender listed in `commands.ownerAllowFrom` can also ask the agent to disable an existing automation by chat.
caveats: Each iPhone can already silence the night on a schedule, so what Happy adds is the daily cap, the urgent or not-urgent split, the label and the pause by chat.

It is not a hard gate for scheduled texts: the message_sending hook that sees `--announce` deliveries lets the message through if the plugin throws or times out, and only the agent's own message tool is gated fail-closed.
The reading of the announce path comes from bundled JavaScript and not a doc page, so confirm it with a throwaway hook before relying on either hook.
No doc lists a job id on message_sending, so each job may have to write its own tag into the text.
No built-in quiet hours or priority classes were found in OpenClaw, so keeping urgent alerts on during a mute depends on this plugin.
The household store does not exist yet, so the counters and the paused-until row are a design and not an installed feature.
The fixed emergency reply (CRT-13) answers an inbound text and must never be held back by quiet hours, caps or a mute.
corrections: reply_payload_sending does not cover --announce on the installed build: the scheduler's announce path sends without a reply-payload hook descriptor and the outbound stage skips that hook when none is supplied. message_sending is the hook that sees those deliveries (the G005 wording already uses it), and it fails open on handler error, so it is a best-effort gate.

The 9 Oct note said switching jobs off needs operator.admin and so cannot be done from

-main; the installed docs also let a sender listed in `commands.ownerAllowFrom` ask the agent to disable an existing automation by chat.
unverified: The announce-path reading comes from bundled JavaScript, not a doc page; confirm with a throwaway hook before relying on either hook.
How the hook learns which job produced a text; no doc lists a job id on message_sending, so the job may have to write its own tag into the text.
Whether a scheduled iPhone Do Not Disturb can silence only Happy's thread; Apple's page confirmed scheduling and allowed people, not per-contact silencing.
The home-store plugin does not exist yet; the paused-until row is a design, not an installed feature.
Keeping 'urgent classes' on during a mute depends on the planned notification-policy plugin (G001); no built-in quiet hours or priority classes were found.
Switching the brief to trip context (destination weather) is a prompt idea with no source.
safety: Both halves only hold back or pause Happy's own unprompted texts; neither adds a recipient, a tool or a data source. Urgent classes keep passing during a mute, and switching everything off stays an operator action.

name: Local classifier calls (decision_evaluate with an on-device ONNX model)
description: A way to ask a small on-device model a yes/no, pick-one or score question (is this email urgent, does this text look like a bank statement, is this reply fine for an eight-year-old) and get a typed answer with a probability, with no cloud call. It is the missing piece behind the catalog's privacy gate, urgent-mail gate and kids classifier, and it does not depend on the skipped local-LLM milestone.
example: Trigger: the school-mail reader's hook asks one Boolean question about a new email's subject and first lines; only a probability above the threshold reaches the URGENT path.
how:
Release 2026.9.7 adds the decisionModel role and the core decision_evaluate tool, and plugins can call the same runtime from a hook through api.runtime.decisions.evaluate. The local provider is the @openclaw/onnx plugin, installed pinned to the Gateway version (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7): zero-shot classifier presets on CPU in a separate worker process, with models fetched only by an explicit download command and checked against fixed hashes. Config is agents.defaults.decisionModel (or per agent) plus plugins.entries.onnx. Call it from the in-house hooks (F084 gate, F055 reader, later the F072 kids filters) rather than granting the tool to

-main.
depends_on: The co-versioned plugin release pinned at install (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7), proven to load and pass its probe command on a test profile before any gate relies on it
A small labelled test set per question, so false positives and misses are measured before a gate relies on it
caveats: The installed 2026.9.7 docs still call the ONNX and TypeSafe plugins unpublished candidates, but the npm registry lists an @openclaw/onnx 2026.9.7 build whose requirement is openclaw 2026.9.7 or later. The latest tag (2026.10.1) needs a newer Gateway, so the version must be pinned at install. The plugin is weeks old; treat it as experimental.
These are generic zero-shot classifiers, not child-safety models; they can score and shortlist, but a kids deployment still needs its own evaluation and a second gate.
There is no fallback to the chat model when the decision provider is unavailable, and an unavailable result is not a 'no', so every gate has to fail closed.
The other provider, TypeSafe's hosted model, is a cloud service and out of scope.

Apple's on-device model (the bundled apple-fm plugin) is not a substitute today: it is documented only as a setup and utility model for short internal tasks such as session titles, and none of the installed pages that mention it describe a classification use.
Each encoded input, rubric included, must fit 512 tokens and longer input is rejected rather than truncated, so a gate has to send a subject and first lines, or chunk a document itself.
Returned probabilities are model estimates, not calibrated; thresholds have to come from the labelled test set.
safety: This strengthens the architecture: the decision runs locally and returns a typed value rather than prose, and the hook, not the model, applies the threshold; the docs say results do not grant permission to act. Hostile text can still shift a score, so a classifier is a filter in front of a hard rule, never the rule itself. No data leaves the Mac.
unverified: Whether @openclaw/onnx 2026.9.7 installs and loads cleanly on this 2026.9.7 host; the installed docs predate its publication and describe only a source-checkout route
Classifier accuracy on this family's school mail and on kids' questions
Memory and CPU use of the worker process
Which host the model download command fetches weights from and which egress rule it needs

name: Undo the last thing (a change journal with inverses)
description: A parent can say 'undo that' after Happy adds the wrong reminder, list item or calendar entry, or overwrites a household fact, and Happy reverses its own last write after showing what it will reverse. It covers only Happy's own writes from the last 24 hours; anything already sent (a text, an email, a print job) cannot be recalled.
example: Tony texts 'undo that' after Happy replaced the furnace filter size in the household facts with the wrong one. Happy shows the old value, waits for a yes and restores it.
how:
OpenClaw has no undo for tool effects. The only rewind found in the installed docs is the Control UI's session rewind, an admin-scoped action that moves the transcript back and does not mention reversing what tools did. So this is in-house work. Each in-house write tool (the household store, the Reminders bridge, the calendar-write server, the hook that pins reminders made with the automations tool) writes a journal row from inside the tool, where the before-state is known: who asked, when, which tool, and the inverse call. The after_tool_call hook only observes results and cannot supply the before-state. An undo_last tool on

-main, limited by a before_tool_call hook to the requester's own rows from the last 24 hours, shows the row, waits for a yes, then runs the inverse: restore the old value or delete the new row, un-complete or delete the reminder item, delete the calendar event Happy created, or 'openclaw automations remove' for a scheduled reminder. A saved note is undone by editing the line in MEMORY.md (F041); derived memory is an operator job with 'openclaw memory forget'. Every write reply ends by saying whether it can be undone.
depends_on: F031 household store
F030 Reminders bridge
F007 reminders
F010 calendar write, if built
G006 audit digest (can share the journal table)
caveats: Sent things cannot be recalled: a text to the other parent, an email to the owner, a print job, a Sonos announcement. The reply has to say so at the time of sending.

Only Happy's own writes are covered. If a parent has since edited the same reminder or event on a phone, the inverse could overwrite that edit, so the tool should refuse when the item changed after Happy wrote it.
'openclaw memory forget' deletes at once with no confirmation unless --dry-run is passed, and it keeps the source transcripts; it is not something to hand to a chat command.
The phone already has undo for what a person does by hand. This covers only what Happy did on their behalf.

The 9 Oct Reminders bridge (F030) was specified as list, add and complete with no delete. Undo needs a delete, so that delete must accept only item ids that Happy's own journal recorded as created by Happy, enforced inside the tool and not left to the model.

The entry's own example ('I meant Thursday, not Tuesday') is a correction, which the same write tool already handles with a second write. The journal earns its place for overwritten household facts, where the old value would otherwise be gone, and as the audit trail.
safety:
Undo reverses a write that the same person's agent made, so it adds no new reach: no new recipient and no new data source. The hook keys on the requester's handle and blocks on error. It lives on

-main, which does not read untrusted web content, and it cannot touch the other parent's rows.
unverified: That no built-in undo for tool effects exists anywhere in 2026.9.7. This rests on a search of the installed docs for undo, rewind and revert, not on reading the source.
Whether the Reminders command-line tool and the calendar server return stable item ids that an inverse can target; neither is installed yet.
A wider search of the installed docs in this review (undo, revert, checkpoint) also found no undo for tool effects; the dist source was still not read.

name: Personal-agent behaviour checks in the eval suite (Happy scorecard)
description: A few fixed test cases, added to the existing eval suite, that check Happy on the behaviours OpenClaw's own personal-agent pack checks. Four apply today: no secret echo, no fake "done", honest partial-failure reports, and keeping pending apart from done. Reminder round trip, preference recall and stopping after a denied approval are added as those tools land. They run against the eval clones after each change. The shipped pack itself cannot run on this install.
example: Tony runs the eval suite after a deploy and reads the pass or fail lines for these cases before texting the family that something new is on.
how:
The shipped pack is out of reach: it needs an OpenClaw source checkout and `OPENCLAW_ENABLE_PRIVATE_QA_CLI=1`, drives the synthetic qa-channel with a mock model, and the Homebrew npm install has no qa directory. Build instead: write the ten scenario themes as promptfoo cases in happy-config/evals against the `

-main-eval` clones through promptfoo's `openclaw` provider (the roadmap E0 harness), with fixtures standing in for reminders and approvals, and store the pass rate next to the smoke results. Operator tooling only.
depends_on: roadmap E0 eval harness (exists)
F007 and F041, so the reminder and memory cases have something to test
caveats: The upstream pack with a mock model measures the plumbing; a promptfoo port measures the real model and costs tokens on every run.
Ten cases is a regression tripwire, not a benchmark. Anthropic's guidance is to start from 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and to read the transcripts, not only the scores.
Eval clones must keep messaging tools denied, or a reminder test texts the family.
The docs say not to point the upstream pack at live chat services or real accounts.

Several of the ten themes have nothing to exercise on Happy today: no tool is approval-gated, so there is nothing to deny; reminders need F007; preference recall needs F041; thread routing and diagnostics artifacts are developer-surface checks. Start with the themes that apply now (no secret echo, no fake "done", honest partial failure, pending versus done) and add the rest as the tools land.
safety: Runs only against eval clones with fake users and fake secrets; no live channel, no real memory, no accounts.
unverified: That the scenario YAML files are readable in the upstream repository at the 2026.9.7 tag (not fetched).
How promptfoo's tool-trajectory assertions behave against 2026.9.7 (an open item in the roadmap).
