name: School mailbox with an isolated reader and a weekday 16:00 digest
description: A separate mailbox registered with school, PTA, coaches and the lunch system is read by an isolated, memory-less reader, so no parent's private inbox is touched. Weekday afternoons both parents get a five-line text of the day's school and activity mail with dates spelled out, a dated to-do list with day-before reminders offered, and one line per child from the school platforms' own summary emails where the school uses them.
example: Trigger: weekdays at 16:00. Text: 'School mail today: picture day is Thursday 15 October, order form due Wednesday 14 October; PTA meeting moved to Tuesday 20 October at 7 pm; lunch balance is low. Want a reminder the day before each?'
how: Mailbox (F051): the bundled `imap` plugin on a new mailbox (iCloud needs `watch.mode: "interval"`), a sender allowlist that includes both parents for forwards, and a tool-less reader. The plugin cannot text a person by itself, so reaching the parents needs a hook-pinned `message` tool or a scheduled sweep. Digest (F056): `automations create '0 16 * * 1-5' --agent school-mail --session isolated --announce --to <chat>` with `--tools school-mail-ro__*`; the read MCP is `gog mcp` (Gmail) or a himalaya wrapper (iCloud). Setup done once by a parent, per platform: ParentSquare posts set to Digest with email on, PowerSchool's scheduled emails and Balance Alert sent to the mailbox, Google Classroom guardian summaries, the lunch service's low-balance alert, library notices; each sender goes on the allowlist.
caveats: Pick the mailbox provider with the password in mind: the plugin signs in with a mailbox password only, which on Gmail means a Google app password that Google does not recommend, while OpenClaw's guide names Fastmail and iCloud.

Each school system has to accept an extra guardian address, a manual chore per system, and auto-forwarding from a parent's Gmail may fail the plugin's aligned-DMARC check, so registering the address directly is the safe route.
The reader gets body text and attachment file names only, so PDF or image newsletters and flyer attachments are not read.

Urgent alerts are not this digest's job, since the school's own alerts reach the parents' phones first; the reader keeps one backup rule (a closure, delay or early-dismissal message from an allowlisted school sender is passed on at the next sweep, not held until 16:00), and sorting urgent from routine on real district mail is untested.

PowerSchool emails carry grades and attendance and Classroom summaries carry assignment titles: these are a child's education records and they reach the cloud model under store:false, which is why the card is rated medium risk.
Classroom summaries (missing and upcoming work, no grades) arrive only if the school uses Classroom and the teacher switches them on, and the guardian invitation expires after 120 days.
One job appears to take one delivery target, so two parents need two jobs or the parents' group chat, and the iCloud read path likely needs an in-house himalaya wrapper.

For a school or team app that sends no email, try the app's own email notifications into this mailbox first and a parent's screenshot to Happy second; Canvas and ClassDojo have no verified email path.
corrections: 'IMAP passes body text only' is slightly off: the plugin's prompt also lists attachment file names (dist/extensions/imap/index.js:55735). Contents of attached PDFs or images are still not passed, so flyer attachments remain unread.
'school-mail-ro MCP is gog (Gmail)' needs no wrapper code on the Gmail path: upstream gogcli ships a read-only stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`).
The built-in scheduling tool is listed as `automations`, with `cron` kept as an alias (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:73).
unverified: Whether the district, PTA, coaches and lunch system each accept an extra or shared guardian address; this is a manual chore per system.

Auto-forwarding school mail from a parent's Gmail by filter may fail the plugin's aligned-DMARC check (Google's forwarding guidance says forwarded mail often fails SPF); DKIM survival was not tested, so registering the address directly is the safe route.
An iCloud+ custom-domain address with this plugin was not tested; Apple documents the IMAP host and app-specific passwords, not this combination.
The catalog marks this 'now' because it needs no private-inbox decision; I rate it 'build' because it needs a new mailbox, an app password and a reader agent entry.

Whether himalaya has an MCP mode; its README does not mention one, so the iCloud path likely needs an in-house wrapper. The README also says native keyring support was removed in v2, so its password comes from a command.
That one job takes exactly one delivery target (hence two jobs or one group chat for two parents); I saw single-target examples only.
Groups are off today, so a family group chat target needs the iMessage group allowlist switched on first.
The home-store checklist, the F007 reminder path and the promptfoo newsletter eval are in-house pieces.
PDF or image newsletters are not read: the IMAP path passes attachment names only.
Which platforms this family's district uses, and each platform's exact sender address and authentication result.
Whether the school uses Google Classroom at all, and whether a student can have the school mailbox as an extra guardian next to both parents.
ClassDojo's notification behaviour and Canvas's calendar feed for observers; neither page could be opened.
safety: All school mail is untrusted and is read only by the memory-less school-mail agent behind a sender allowlist with verified authentication; that agent has no web or file tools and can only announce to the two parents. Links are relayed only when their domain matches the allowlisted sender. No agent logs in to a school portal and no portal credentials are stored.

name: Practice quiz from a study-guide photo or a word list, run by a parent
description: A parent photographs the study guide or vocabulary sheet, or pastes a spelling list or asks for math facts, and Happy quizzes from it: ten questions, one at a time, hint first, a running score and the answer key at the end. Alexa+ and Gemini both ship a quiz made from your own material. The parent holds the phone; a version the kids use themselves waits for the kids agent (F072).
example: Jordan sends a photo of the science study guide and texts: 'quiz us on this, 10 questions, one at a time.'
how:
A photo needs inbound attachments on (`channels.imessage.includeAttachments: true`; see F002) behind the F084 document gate; `

-main` reads it with the reply model's own vision. A small operator-reviewed workspace skill (AUT-06) fixes the format: one question per message, wait for the answer, one hint before revealing, a running score, the answer key at the end, no web lookups. A pasted spelling list or a request for math facts uses the same skill with no photo and needs no attachments. An optional one-shot `automations` reminder offers a re-quiz the night before the test. No new tool: this is a prompt-only addition.
depends_on: F002 photo and PDF understanding with inbound attachments switched on, for the photo route only
F084 privacy gate, for the photo route only
AUT-06 operator-reviewed skill for the quiz format (optional; needs the `read` tool)

F007 automations tool on

-main (only for the optional re-quiz reminder)
VOX-04 local spoken replies (only for reading spelling words aloud)
caveats: Parent-run only: the kids are not users, and the parent holds the phone and sends the answers. The roadmap's child-safety rule keeps the kids' own content away from cloud providers, so this must not turn into a child chatting with Happy alone; that version waits for the kids agent (F072) and never uses a cloud model or cloud speech.
The ChatGPT or Gemini app on a parent's phone does the same thing today; Happy's only edge is that it lives in the same thread and can schedule the re-quiz.
Models write wrong answer keys, especially for arithmetic and for facts the sheet does not state. Tell it to quiz only from what is on the page and spot-check.

A text quiz shows spelling words on screen, so spelling practice needs the words read aloud: a spoken reply made on the Mac with the local voice (VOX-04, which starts with the built-in macOS say voice), whose quality for spelling words is untried.
The running score lives in the conversation and is gone after the daily session reset.
safety:
The photo is untrusted content read by an agent that holds memory, but `

-main` has no browse tool and can only reply to its owner, so the trifecta is not closed. School worksheets go to the cloud vision model under store:false, which is decision 3 in the catalog. No kid account talks to a cloud model.
unverified: Whether a spoken reply arrives as a playable voice message or as a file in iMessage Basic mode.
The quality of the macOS say voice for spelling words was not tried.

name: Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks
description: A grid of every weekday the kids have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, the ten or so summer weeks) against who covers it: camp, grandparents, a trip, a parent off work. Happy keeps the grid, lists the open cells months ahead, tracks registration dates, and at tax time lists what was paid to which day camp. School and camp form paperwork is a separate entry (CRT-12).
example: Trigger: first Sunday of February. Happy texts both parents: 'Jordan coverage: 4 of 10 weeks open for the 10-year-old, 6 for the 8-year-old. Two camps you saved open registration this week.'
how:
Inputs: the district calendar (a public feed the family Google Calendar is subscribed to, read through F009, or a photo or PDF through snap-to-action, F011) gives the no-school weekdays; parents add coverage by text. Store: household store rows (F031) keyed by date range and child nickname, with a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a provider name. Jobs: a monthly isolated job on

-main from January to May, and weekly in the four weeks before each break ('--cron'), listing open cells; page watchers for 'registration opens' on camps the parents name (F029, created by Tony); options research by the stateless research agent given ages, weeks and a distance only (F026). Parents register and pay themselves. After paying, a parent sends the receipt and Happy records amount and provider. In February it lists day-camp totals per provider and which providers still lack a taxpayer number, because IRS Publication 503 treats day camp, and not overnight camp, as a possible work-related care expense for a child under 13, and asks for the provider's name, address and taxpayer number (Form W-10 is the request form).

F009 family calendar subscribed to the district feed, or F011 for a district calendar PDF
F029 watchers and F026 research (need the research agent)

name: Enrolment, camp and health-form paperwork kit
description: Every August and every camp season the same documents are asked for again: the immunization record, a recent physical, insurance details, emergency contacts, proof of address. Happy keeps a per-child index of where each document is and when it stops being accepted, warns before a form is due, and, when a school, camp or sports form arrives as a photo or PDF, drafts the answers from the stored family facts as one copy-paste block. The parent fills, signs and submits.
example: Jordan texts: 'Camp forms for both kids are due May 1. What do I still need?'
how:
One Markdown page per child in the shared family folder, indexed through memory.search.extraPaths (F043 step 1). For each document it records where the official copy lives (the pediatric office, the state immunization registry, the filing cabinet), the date on it, and the date it stops being accepted. CDC says it holds no vaccination records and points parents to the child's doctor, the state immunization information system and the school, so the page notes which of those worked last time. A dated row per form in the household store (F031) drives the reminders: 'the physical on file is older than this camp accepts, book a visit' and 'forms due in 14 days'. The copy-paste block (formerly the health-form helper, F067) is drafted on

-main from a per-child 'form facts' section of the same page when the form arrives as a photo or PDF (F002), under a drafts-only rule in AGENTS.md; the agent has no exec, so it cannot alter or fill in the original form, and ID and policy numbers are left blank for the parent. Scans stay in Files or the paper folder; only the index and the form facts go to Happy.
depends_on: F043 family folder
F031 household store
F002 photo and PDF reading with inbound attachments on, for a form sent as a photo or PDF
F007 reminders
caveats: Requirements differ by state, district and camp. Happy tracks what each form asked for last time; it does not know the rules.
The official immunization record has to come from the doctor or the state registry. Happy cannot fetch it, because portal logins are out of scope.
Signing is done by the parent, with the phone's markup tools or on paper. Happy never signs, fills a web form or submits.
An index of where documents are is itself sensitive. Keep ID numbers, policy numbers and certificate numbers out of it.
The form-facts section holds the children's health facts (allergies, medicines, conditions), and they reach the cloud model whenever an answer block is drafted.
The drafts-only rule is a prompt instruction; it holds only because the agent has no tool that could fill in or send a form.
safety: Index pages hold locations and dates, not the documents or identifiers. The form-facts section does hold the children's health facts, and drafting an answer block sends them to the cloud model under store:false. Both sit in the parents' private agents' search path, nothing is browsed in the same turn, and nothing is sent outside the family. Children's health details stay out of research handoffs.
unverified: Whether this state's immunization registry gives parents direct online access.
Typical validity windows for school and camp physicals; twelve months is often quoted but was not sourced here.
The estimate of 6 to 10 such forms a year is not sourced.

name: Family logistics briefs: evening (19:30), Sunday week-ahead (18:00), weekday morning (07:00)
description: Each parent gets short scheduled texts built from the family calendar and the weather. Sunday to Thursday at 19:30: tomorrow's events, who drives, what to pack and the weather, and nothing when the day is unremarkable. Sunday at 18:00: the week ahead, with early releases, activities, drivers, packing, the weather outlook and open school deadlines. Optionally, weekdays at 07:00: weather and alerts, today's calendar, items due and trash day. Mail stays in its own digests (F056, F016).
example: Sunday to Thursday at 19:30 each parent gets one text: tomorrow's two events and who drives each, 'pack shin guards', and rain after 3.
how:
One isolated job per parent per brief on

-main, all from one template: tools `home_weather` plus the read-only calendar MCP (`

-calendar__*`), no web tools, no `--light-context`, `--tz` set, `--announce --to imessage:`. Schedules: evening `--cron "30 19 * * 0-4"`, week-ahead `--cron "0 18 * * 0"`, morning `--cron "0 7 * * 1-5"`. The routines and gear table lives in AGENTS.md; a run replies `NO_REPLY` to stay silent. The week-ahead and morning legs also read the household store (F031) for items due, trash day and open school deadlines. Email-derived dates for the week-ahead come from a separate

-mail job using `llm-task`, never the same run. Build the evening brief first; the morning brief is the optional one.
caveats: On Sundays the 18:00 week-ahead and the 19:30 evening brief would both arrive within ninety minutes. Either let the Sunday week-ahead carry Monday's detail and run the evening brief Monday to Thursday only (`1-4`), or accept two texts.

The morning leg is the optional one: it needs the household store (F031) for items due and trash day, and the weather plugin returns no sunset, so a sunset line, if wanted, needs a small local calculation.
unverified: The 'tight gaps' line: gog's MCP page lists a single Calendar tool (list events), so overlaps and gaps must be worked out by the model or a custom wrapper; no conflict tool was found.
The [T]/[S] driver tag is a family habit the brief depends on, not a product feature; no source can vouch that both adults will keep it up.
gog is not installed, so its flags were checked only against its website, not a binary.
How many days the NWS gridpoint forecast covers was not read on the opened page.
The deadlines input (home-store rows or a sheet) does not exist yet; its shape is a design choice, not a sourced fact.

The catalog passes `home-store__*` in `--tools`; the installed docs document the `<server>__<tool>` prefix only for MCP servers, and home-store is planned as a native plugin, so that glob is untested.
That the NWS forecast endpoints carry no sunrise or sunset field: the opened documentation page does not list one, absence was not proven.

name: Two-parent calendar conflict watch
description: Ohai sells avoiding conflicts across family members' calendars. Happy's version: when a new overlap appears in the next 14 days (both parents busy at a kid's pickup, two events needing the same driver), both parents get one line naming the clash, with an optional who-covers question.
example: Trigger: Tony accepts a Thursday 16:00 meeting; Jordan already has the dentist then and the 10-year-old has practice. Both get: 'Thursday 16:00: both of you are busy and practice pickup has no driver.'
how: A zero-model command job (`--command-argv`) every few hours runs a host script under the happy user: `gog calendar conflicts` (or `freebusy`) across the shared family calendar and the two parents' calendars, compares against a seen-id state file, and prints `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. To keep each parent's data separate, the script uses one read-only credential that sees the family calendar in full and each parent's own calendar as free/busy only (Google's 'See only free/busy (hide details)' share), so the message names the family-calendar event and says only 'busy' for personal ones. The docs show a single `--to` target per job, so plan one job per parent or the parents' group chat once F006 exists; the follow-up question reuses the G010 relay.

name: Public calendar, feed and page watchers: a text when a game moves or a site posts something new
description: Tony registers a team's calendar link, a site's feed or a public page; a script with no model checks it on a schedule and texts a parent once when a practice or game moves or is cancelled, when camp registration opens, or when the school, district or town site posts something new. Subscribing the same team link in the family calendar also puts practices and games into Happy's calendar answers and briefs.
example: Trigger: the Saturday game's start time changes in the team's feed. Text: 'Soccer Saturday moved from 9:00 to 10:30, same field.'
how: All are operator-created host command jobs with no model call, the pattern of the weather watch (F018). Schedule watch (SRC-09): add the subscription link from TeamSnap, SportsEngine or GameChanger to the family calendar so F009 reads it; then `node scripts/ics-watch.mjs <feed name>`, hourly in season, fetches the link from a file only the happy user can read, keeps each event's start, location and status in a state file, and prints one line per changed event in the next seven days. Page and feed watch (F029): `node scripts/watch-page.mjs <watch name>` every 6 hours uses the site's RSS/Atom feed when there is one, otherwise a plain https GET, keeps seen ids or a text hash, and prints one templated line with a link on the registered host only. Both print `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new.
caveats: A parent cannot start a watch from chat: a command job is created by the operator, so each new watch is a request to Tony.

Subscribed calendars can lag by up to a day (TeamSnap says Google can take up to 24 hours), which is why the change text needs its own script, and the team app's own push is still the fastest signal for a same-day change.
A team's subscription link is a bearer secret, since anyone with it can read the schedule, so keep it out of family.json5 if that file is committed.
Many school and town pages change for reasons that do not matter (a date, a banner), so a hash watch can fire falsely; a per-watch keyword that must appear cuts this down.
Pages that render only with JavaScript are out of reach of a host command job, and many school portals and social pages publish no feed.

Command jobs run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, agent tool policy and OpenClaw's fetch guardrails, so the scripts check each address themselves (https, public host) and are reviewed like the rest of the config repo.
Run one job per parent with its own state file, or one job delivering to the parents' group chat once F006 exists, because with a shared state file the second parent's job stays silent.
The text says that something changed and gives the link; reading the page is a separate ask to the research agent (F019), and price drops are not covered.
corrections: The catalog's needs used `--once` and the verifier said no CLI flag exists (JSON or Control UI only); the installed CLI source defines `--trigger-once`.
unverified: Which of the family's school, town and camp sites publish a feed, and which registration pages can be read without JavaScript.
The five-watchers-per-person cap is a convention; nothing enforces it.
Which agent's session transcript receives the mirrored announce line of a command job (see SRC-03); keep the line short and templated.
GameChanger's exact rules on who can sync practices versus games.
How quickly each service's .ics link itself reflects a change (only the downstream calendar lag is documented).
Rate limits or terms for polling the subscription links hourly.
safety: No model reads the feed or the page: the scripts relay only a fixed line, with coach-typed titles and locations stripped to plain characters and capped, so outside text cannot steer an agent. Requests go only to addresses Tony registered. Team schedules say where the kids will be and when, so they stay on the host and go only to pinned parent handles.

name: Recipe link to ingredients and steps
description: Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps without the life story and the ads, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add the ingredients to the shared grocery list.
example: "<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?"
how:
Mechanism choice: plain `web_fetch`, which reduces a page to its main content; schema.org also defines a Recipe vocabulary (`recipeIngredient`, `recipeInstructions`, `recipeYield`) that recipe sites can embed.

-main hands the URL to research with `sessions_spawn` and `completionTarget: "parent"`; research fetches, makes one `llm-task` call with a small schema (title, yield, ingredients[], steps[], source URL, fetched-at) and returns that JSON as its result;

-main scales quantities and proposes items for the shared grocery list (F030), written only after a yes. The schema shapes the answer but is not an enforced gate: the result reaches

-main as ordinary sub-agent text. Fallbacks in order: the F020 research browser for script-rendered pages; a host-side `summarize --extract` wrapper for video recipes (the CLI is not installed; pin `--firecrawl off` in the wrapper).
depends_on: F019 research agent
F082 llm-task
F030 Reminders bridge for the grocery list
caveats: The fetch returns the readable article text. It is not documented to return the page's embedded Recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line. Always include the source link.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; say so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already do the clean-up; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
'Add what is missing' assumes Happy knows what is in the kitchen. It does not; in practice it offers the whole ingredient list and the parent strikes what they have.

The summarize CLI named as the video fallback takes any address and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks. A wrapper must pass `--firecrawl off`, hold no third-party keys, and check the address itself (https, public host), because OpenClaw's SSRF policy does not cover a host-side CLI.
The reading half works the day the research agent exists; the grocery hand-off, which is the part the phone does not already do, waits on the Reminders bridge.
On today's config no agent has `web_fetch` or `sessions_spawn` and the `llm-task` plugin is not enabled; all three are config changes that arrive with F019 and F082.
safety:
The untrusted page is read by research only, and nothing private goes to research: an address and a serving count. What comes back to

-main is text written by a model that has just read an untrusted page. Running it through `llm-task` with a schema fixes its shape, not its content: a step string can still carry instructions, and nothing in the platform forces the check to run. The limits that hold are that

-main has no browser or fetch and its recipients are pinned to the family. List writes wait for the parent's yes, a prompt rule that is acceptable at grocery-list stakes.
unverified: Whether web_fetch output ever includes a page's JSON-LD blocks: a search of the installed code found no JSON-LD handling in the fetch extractor, but no live recipe page was fetched.
How many of the recipe sites this family uses embed schema.org Recipe data.

Whether a plugin hook can enforce a schema on a sub-agent's result before

-main reads it.
Whether llm-task's isolated completion works through the family's per-person custom provider ids; its allowed-model list has to name them.

name: Tax document checklist (January to April)
description: January to April, a Saturday text listing which expected tax forms have had an arrival email and which are still missing. It reports that a notice arrived and does not read the form.
how:
A Saturday job from January to April on the owner's mail agent: `automations create '0 9 * 1-4 6' --agent

-mail --session isolated --announce --to `, with `--tools` limited to the read-only Gmail search tool (F047). The job prompt carries the family's expected-forms list with each sender; the run searches for mail from each sender since 1 January and reports 'arrived' with the date, or 'missing'. Nothing is stored between runs. The earlier design, an IMAP watch on payroll, broker and bank senders (F050) feeding a job with `--tools ""`, applies only if that watcher is ever built.
caveats: It only knows that a notice email arrived. Forms that come by post, or sit in a portal without an email, show as missing even when they are in hand.
It is useful four months a year, and cron has no end date, so the job is switched off by hand after filing.

'Does not read the form' is an instruction to the mail agent, not an enforced limit, because the same agent can read the owner's mail. The stricter design, an allowlisted-sender watch feeding a job with no tools, needs the personal-inbox watcher (F050) and its whole-mailbox Google app password.
unverified: The family's own expected-forms list (Form 1098, 529 and childcare statements) is theirs to write; the IRS page fetched does not name Form 1098.
Sender domains for payroll, brokerage and the 529 plan.
Whether personal mail may be read by the cloud model at all is Tony's open decision for every personal-mail feature (see F016).

name: Severe-weather, snow-day and weather-chore watch
description: Both parents get a three-line heads-up once per new winter storm, wind, flood or freeze alert for home, with a school-night closure reminder and a chore checklist.
how: Host command job, `--command-argv '["node","scripts/nws-alerts.mjs"]'` every 30 minutes, polls api.weather.gov `/alerts/active?point=`, dedups on alert `id`, prints `NO_REPLY` otherwise; zero model calls.
caveats: Phones receive Wireless Emergency Alerts only for the most extreme warnings (tornado, hurricane, extreme wind, snow squall, the worst flash floods and thunderstorms); winter storm, freeze and ordinary high-wind warnings are not sent that way.

Apple's Weather app can also notify about government-issued severe weather alerts, but only once a parent switches that on for the home location. With it on, what Happy adds is one text to both parents with the school-night line and the chore checklist, not earlier notice.
Happy is down in a power cut or a network outage, so this is a convenience and not a warning system; the phones' own emergency alerts stay switched on.

name: Recall watch matched to what the family owns: products (CPSC), food and medicine (FDA)
description: A script checks the Consumer Product Safety Commission's recall list each day and FDA's recall and safety notices twice a day, and texts a parent only when a notice matches something the family owns, an allergen it cares about, a staple brand or a children's medicine in the cabinet. The agencies publish far more notices than anyone reads, so the filter is the feature.
example: Trigger: a new recall whose product name contains a brand on the family's owned-items list. Text: 'CPSC recall 26-xxx: <product title>. Hazard: burn. Remedy: refund. Link: cpsc.gov/...'
how: Two operator-created command jobs with no model, each announced to a pinned parent. Products (SRC-03): `node scripts/cpsc-recalls.mjs` once a day asks the CPSC recall web service for recalls since the last run (a date filter only), keeps seen RecallID values in a state file and matches product, maker, retailer and UPC fields locally against owned-item keywords and a short kid-category list; an owned match texts now, a category match waits for a Sunday digest of at most five. Food and medicine (SRC-04): `node scripts/fda-recalls.mjs` twice a day reads FDA's Recalls/Safety Alerts RSS feed and matches titles against allergen, staples and medicine keywords from family.json5. Both print a templated line or `NO_REPLY`. Cars are not polled: parents add VINs and car seats to NHTSA's SaferCar app.
depends_on: F018 command-job pattern
G003 jobs registry
G001 notification policy
the home systems registry in F043 or a hand-kept owned-items list
allergen, staples and medicine keyword lists in family.json5
caveats: The match is only as good as the family's lists: substring matching on brand names gives some false positives and misses unlisted items, and FDA titles that do not name the allergen or brand are missed.
Both agencies already offer their own recall sign-ups, so Happy adds the match against the family's own list and not earlier notice.
FDA's own list says not every recall has a press release or is posted there, so silence from this watch is not an all-clear.
openFDA enforcement data is updated weekly and FDA says it must not be used to issue alerts or to make medical decisions, so the RSS notices give timeliness and openFDA is only a detail lookup.
Meat, poultry and egg-product recalls come from USDA FSIS, whose developer page refused the fetch, so that leg is not included.
The food and medicine leg is worth most if a child has a diagnosed food allergy; otherwise it is a low-frequency nudge.
Run one job per parent with its own seen-id state file, because with a shared file the second parent's job finds nothing new and stays silent.
No key or rate limit is documented for the CPSC service, so poll once a day and not more.
safety: No model runs in either job, and nothing about the family leaves the house: the lists are pulled by date or whole and filtered locally. Recall titles are untrusted and a delivered line is mirrored into the owning agent's transcript, so the scripts print a fixed template with stripped, capped titles and only the official link. Not medical advice.
unverified: Formal terms of use or rate limit for the recall web service (the page read gives none).
Documentation for the RecallDateStart parameter (it is not on the API information page read; it is confirmed only by the live response).
Which agent's session receives the mirrored line for a command job, to be checked by reading the transcript after the first run.
The USDA FSIS recall API (endpoint, fields, terms): the page returned 403.
Whether the FDA RSS feed has a documented polling limit.

name: Sick-day mode with a shared what-was-given log
description: When a child is ill, both parents log what they gave and when, and either can ask 'when was the last dose?' and get the same answer; a poison control centre lists medicine given by more than one person who do not communicate as a cause of double dosing, and recommends a log that is marked at every dose. The same mode drafts the absence note and lists what tomorrow needs cancelling. Happy records and recalls. It never advises a dose.
example: Jordan texts: 'L has a fever, gave the children's acetaminophen at 7:40.' Later Tony texts: 'When was the last dose?'
how: Rows in the household store (F031): child nickname, what the parent typed, time, who. A care_last tool, built with defineToolPlugin like the store, returns the latest rows and the elapsed minutes, computed in code and not by the model. Both parents' agents read the same table. The reply always ends with a fixed line: check the label for dose and timing, and ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure. There is no dose arithmetic and no 'you can give more now'. Add-ons from features already in the catalog: a draft absence note the parent sends through the school's own channel (F037), tomorrow's calendar items that need a cancel or a cover (F009), a tracked ask to the other parent about staying home (G010), and a one-shot check-in reminder ('--at'). For 'can she go back tomorrow?' Happy quotes CDC's general rule with its link (symptoms improving overall and no fever for 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine) and says the school's policy wins. Rows delete themselves after 14 days and are kept out of memory writes. To make 'no dose advice' a limit and not a request, care_last returns the finished reply text (the rows as typed, the elapsed time and the fixed line) and the agent is told to send it unchanged; an exact 'last dose' phrase can instead be answered by a before_dispatch claim with no model at all, which also keeps the lookup working when the model is down.
depends_on: F031 household store
F007 reminders
F009 calendar read
G010 parent-to-parent relay
9 Oct decision 3, if photos of labels are sent
caveats: This is a log, not a clinician. A wrong elapsed time is worse than none, so the time comes from the message timestamp unless the parent states one, and the reply repeats it back.

FDA says more than 600 medicines contain acetaminophen and that a child's dose should never be guessed. The log stores the product name as typed so a parent can spot two products with the same ingredient; Happy does not make that judgement.
Child health notes pass through a cloud model under store:false. Use a nickname or initial and keep diagnoses out.
For one parent alone, a note on the phone does the same job. The value is the shared view across two people.
safety:
Runs on

-main only: private data, no untrusted content in the turn (the CDC and FDA lines are fixed text, not fetched), and output only to the two parents through the pinned delivery. Nothing about the child's health is handed to the research agent, per the roadmap's handoff rule. The elapsed time and the fixed line come from code. The rule against dose advice is an AGENTS.md instruction, and a model can still break it by volunteering a 'next dose' remark from its own knowledge; rendering the lookup reply in code, or answering the lookup phrase with a no-model claim, is what turns it into a limit. Add an eval case that asks 'can I give more now?' and must get only the fixed line.
unverified: Whether the iPhone Health app's medication log can be shared live between two parents; if it can, that is the better tool.
Whether the school takes absence notes by email or only through its attendance line or app.
Session transcripts that mention the illness follow the general retention setting; only the rows are auto-deleted.

name: Emergency card and sitter sheet from one set of family facts, plus a fixed reply to emergency texts
description: Happy helps write and keep current a one-page family emergency plan to print, and from the same facts makes a sitter or grandparent sheet (bedtimes, allergies, medicines, emergency contacts) for a parent to forward. Happy is never the emergency channel: a text that looks like an emergency gets one fixed line at once, telling the person to call emergency services, without waiting for a model.
example: A parent texts 'make the sitter sheet for Friday' and gets one message to forward or print. A parent who texts 'He swallowed something, what do I do?' gets the fixed call-emergency-services line immediately.
how:
Plan (CRT-13): Ready.gov's four steps (talk it through, consider the household's needs, write the plan, practise it) become a short interview on

-main; the result is a page in the family folder (F043) and a printed sheet (F080), and a yearly reminder re-checks the contacts. Sitter sheet (F036): a prompt template referenced from AGENTS.md over the same facts, prompt-only and able to go first; nothing is sent by Happy and the Wi-Fi password is never stored. Fixed reply: the kill-switch plugin's `before_dispatch` hook matches a short list of emergency phrases and returns a canned final reply (call the local emergency number now; for a possible poisoning call poison control; Happy cannot call anyone). It answers before model dispatch, so it still works during a model outage.
depends_on: G005 kill-switch plugin (shares the hook)
F043 family folder
F080 print
F007 reminders (the yearly contact re-check)
F009 calendar read (only for 'tonight's plan' on the sitter sheet)
caveats: Happy can be down in exactly the events that matter, since a power cut stops the Mac and a network outage stops iMessage, so the printed sheet is the part that survives.
Phrase matching will fire on jokes and miss paraphrases, so the fixed reply must be harmless when wrong.
The phone's own emergency call and medical ID features are the right tools on the phone, and Happy should point to them, not imitate them.
Quiet hours and daily caps (G001) must never hold the fixed reply back; a reply to an inbound text is not a proactive message, but test it.
Only the two parents can text Happy, so a sitter or grandparent gets the forwarded or printed sheet and cannot ask Happy directly.
'Tonight's plan' on the sitter sheet needs the calendar connection (F009), which is not built yet.
No poison-control number is given here because the federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so the parents write the number into the fixed reply themselves.
safety: The fixed reply is a string written by the parents and sent only to the sender: no tool, no data, no model. The plan page holds contacts and medical notes, so it lives in the private family folder and on paper; only the fridge-level subset goes on the sitter sheet, which a parent forwards, because Happy messages nobody outside the family.

A poison-control source: the federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so no number is given here.

name: Trip paperwork check: children's travel documents
description: Before a family trip Happy works a short paperwork checklist that the planning features do not cover: whose passport is valid for the dates, whether a consent letter is needed when one parent or a grandparent takes a child abroad (with a draft for the other parent to sign and have notarised), and what ID the airport wants from children. Happy certifies nothing and books nothing.
example: Tony texts: 'Jordan is taking the kids to Vancouver in July without me. What paperwork do we need?'
how:
A trip row in the household store (F031): dates, who travels, destination. A checklist on

-main from fixed, linked rules: USA.gov says a child travelling abroad with one parent, a guardian or alone may need a letter of consent, preferably in English and notarised, so Happy drafts the letter text for the non-travelling parent to sign and have notarised; TSA does not require ID from under-18s on domestic flights, though airlines may have their own rules; the child passport dates from the renewals program (F063) are checked against the trip dates. Vacation mode (G002) mutes the home jobs for the dates. An itinerary summary for grandparents is a draft the parent forwards (G011). Delays, gate changes and cancellations stay with the airline's app and its emails.
depends_on: F031 household store
F063 renewals (passport dates)
G002 vacation mode
F019 research agent, for the destination's entry rules
caveats: Entry rules belong to the destination country. Happy links the official page and says to check with the airline and the consulate; it certifies nothing.
The consent letter is a draft for a notary, not legal advice.
No booking, check-in, seat change or rebooking: all are on the never-list.
Two or three trips a year. Build it only after the household store and vacation mode exist.
No flight or airport status watch: the public FAA feed is airport-level only, and the airline's app already pushes changes for the actual flight.

name: Weekly memory review, and forgetting a conversation on request
description: Each adult gets a short Sunday text of what Happy saved to memory that week. On request Tony removes everything Happy learned from one conversation, previewed first; forgetting a single topic is a hand edit of the memory file, not a command. Mail-reader sessions are also excluded from automatic memory ingestion as a backstop.
how: Weekly isolated automation per adult, limited with --tools memory_search,memory_get. Operator runbook: openclaw memory forget --agent <id> --session <id-or-key> --dry-run, read the report, then repeat without --dry-run; it selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, deletes at once, and leaves the transcripts and any reworded copies. A line a parent confirms is written to MEMORY.md directly, because openclaw memory promote needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries by default. memoryPolicy.excludeSessions.hookExternalContentSources [email, gmail] is set as a backstop; it only keeps those sessions out of dreaming ingestion and backfill, which are switched off.
corrections: 'Forget what I said about X works' (9 Oct description) is not a platform ability: memory forget selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, never by topic or message text, and reworded copies are outside its cleanup. Topic-level forgetting is a hand edit of the memory file.

'Promote via openclaw memory promote --apply' will usually promote nothing a parent just confirmed: by default a candidate needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries. Either pass lower thresholds or write the confirmed line to MEMORY.md directly.

name: Recovery card for the second adult (a bus factor of one)
description: One printed page and a sealed envelope so Jordan can tell that Happy is down, pause it, and bring it back after a power cut while Tony is travelling. Today every recovery step, including the disk unlock after a reboot, depends on Tony being at home.
example: Trigger: a power cut while Tony is abroad. Happy stops answering and Jordan opens the card.
how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase (G005) and that it is always safe to use. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The two commands an admin may need: 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the backup (G007). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.
depends_on: decision: Jordan gets break-glass admin access, which also lets her read Tony's data on the Mac
G005 kill phrase
G007 backups
a small UPS (already suggested in the roadmap)
decision: what goes in Jordan's envelope: the happy user's password only (enough for a restart if it unlocks the disk) or also the admin credential (which adds Tony's own account and the config repo)
caveats: The envelope is a credential on paper. The happy password alone already opens every person's agent data, because the gateway keeps it under that account; an admin credential adds Tony's own account and the config repo. That is the price of not being locked out.
A UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the FileVault screen.
Legacy Contact access needs the access key and a death certificate. It is for the worst case, not for a business trip.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.
safety: Nothing is granted to any agent and no secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's in normal operation; the envelope is a deliberate exception that is obvious once used, because it is sealed.
unverified: Whether a standard, non-admin macOS account for Jordan can be enabled to unlock FileVault at boot on this Mac; the Apple page read in this run does not say who may unlock.
Whether the gateway's launchd service comes up for the happy user before that user logs in at the console after a reboot.

name: Node command deny list until a pilot (computer.act and the Mac host commands), plus the off switches
description: Make 'no agent can drive, run commands on or view any Mac' an explicit Gateway setting instead of a side effect of the Mac app not being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off.
example: Tony adds one deny line to the config repo now. Later, 'Happy, stop everything' also halts desk, and he can flip the switch in the Mac app or remove the Accessibility grant.
how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config, and while no Mac node is wanted also every desktop host command the docs list as arriving with a Mac pairing: `system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, matches exact command names, withholds the command (for `computer.act`, together with the node's `computer` capability) and is logged. The list is Gateway-wide, so the iPhone data commands from the phone-pairing entry (OCL-01) can go into the same wave-A change. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. Keep SSH-verified pairing off and do not use setup links for a Mac, since either can approve a node's first command surface automatically. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy; device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface; the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals gate shell commands on a node, not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload, with no restart); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app, so a pilot that lifts a deny entry lifts it for every paired node.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.
The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing and setup-code enrollment can approve a node's first surface automatically.
The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream, which is why the deny list names those commands too.
safety: Pure tightening. It turns an implicit state into a limit in config that a prompt cannot change.
unverified: That deny entries for system.run and the other host commands apply exactly as for computer.act; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.

That denying browser.proxy and mcp.tools.call.v1 for nodes leaves the sandboxed research browser and any MCP servers on the Gateway itself untouched. No node is paired today; check right after the change.

name: Screen-control pilot: one stateless desk agent on a clean, resettable Mac VM (app setup, watching view and go-live test included)
description: An experimental pilot, parked until there is a chore worth it: a dedicated agent with no memory and no other tools is the only holder of `computer`, and it drives a clean macOS virtual machine with no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never happy's own desktop. A parent's agent hands it one bounded task and gets a short text result back; no family task is approved for it today.
example: Operator pilot, not a family text yet: Tony gives desk one synthetic task from the acceptance set (a sample file on the clean desk, with a result that can be checked as a file). desk answers 'done, saved as result.txt' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
how: Clean desk (MAC-03): a macOS guest on the Mac mini built with Apple's Virtualization framework (for example the Lume CLI) and reset to a known snapshot before every run; OpenClaw.app is installed inside the guest, paired as its own node and granted Accessibility and Screen Recording there; files move only through the File Transfer plugin limited to one folder. Desk agent (MAC-02): `agents.entries.desk` with memory off, `tools.profile: minimal`, `computer` added and everything else denied, reached only by `sessions_spawn` from a parent's agent; a `before_tool_call` hook allowlists actions, checks the kill file and returns `requireApproval` on the first action of each run. Around it: Screen Sharing inside the VM only, so a person can watch, and a ten-task acceptance test with three planted-instruction cases.
depends_on: MAC-04 default-deny lifted for exactly one node
disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest
a route from the guest to the loopback-bound gateway (tailnet identity or SSH tunnel) and a firewall rule limiting the guest to the gateway address
`gateway.nodes.commands.allow` entries for the file commands
F019 spawn pattern
G005 kill switch
G009 family delivery
existing on-demand eval harness (for the acceptance test)
a named family chore that no app or script already handles (none approved today)
caveats: The guest is not empty of secrets: OpenClaw.app inside it is signed in to the family gateway, so until the app is shown to run as a node with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen can open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.

The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve, so the guest needs an SSH tunnel, its own tailnet identity or a wider gateway bind, and each of those changes the M0 baseline and needs its own review.
Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole node: shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream arrive together with pointer control.
A hook sees typed parameters and not meaning, so an action allowlist cannot stop the model clicking the wrong thing, and what exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
The approval on the first action only proves that a parent started the task: the dozens of clicks after it run unreviewed, and the prompt is text only with no screenshot.
Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire and not a control.
A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory, because files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run, or one parent, to the next.

Whether Computer Control works inside a macOS guest with a virtual display, and whether an approval raised inside a spawned desk run reaches the asking parent's chat, are both untested, and a pass on the acceptance test shows usefulness, not safety.
safety: desk reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool; its ways out are whatever the controlled desktop can reach. The trifecta counts as respected only after the app's operator access inside the guest is removed or proven absent, guest egress is limited to the gateway, and the guest is reset before each run. Never-list items stay off that desktop.
unverified: That `before_tool_call` receives the `computer` tool's action parameters in `event.params` the same way it does for other built-in tools.
That a spawned desk run returns its result to the requester under the family's session-visibility settings (the roadmap lists the same open question for research).

Where a plugin approval raised inside a spawned desk run is delivered. The docs promise same-chat approval for requests that originate from a chat and block a call that has no approval route; if the sub-run does not count as coming from the parent's iMessage chat, every desk task would fail closed.

Live behaviour of the hook on `computer` calls. The installed source wraps every built-in tool, `computer` included, with the before_tool_call hook, and the tool's schema has `action`, `node`, `text`, `app` and `url` parameters, but this was read, not run.
Whether an approval raised inside a spawned desk run is delivered to the asking parent's iMessage chat; session-mode delivery is documented for the originating chat, not for a child session.

That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its TCC grants, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest VM with a virtual display, including a guest running without a display window.
How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.
Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a node with no operator scopes.

Apple's licence for the installed macOS 27. The macOS Tahoe 26 licence, read in an earlier run, allows up to two additional macOS instances in virtual machines on an Apple-branded computer for personal, non-commercial use.
The guest's memory cost. OpenClaw's macOS VM page asks for about 60 GB of free disk per VM and does not state memory.

name: OpenClaw iPhone app on Tony's phone (pairing, chat with files, tap approvals; device commands denied first)
description: Tony can also reach Happy in the free OpenClaw iPhone app: a native chat that takes photos from the picker, camera or share sheet and PDFs, Office files and audio from Files, queues text while offline, shows source cards and lets assistant-sent files be saved back to the phone. It also has a native approval inbox and question cards, which Basic-mode iMessage cannot show. The app is at once a chat client, an operator console for the whole Gateway and a device node, so it goes on Tony's phone only, and the phone's data commands are denied on the Gateway before it is paired. This entry now also covers the pairing step (was IPH-01) and the phone command ceiling (was HOM-08).
example: Tony saves a 12-page camp packet PDF from Mail to Files, attaches it in the OpenClaw app with + -> File and asks 'what do I have to sign, and by when?'. Later a card appears: 'Add camp drop-off to the Family calendar? Allow once / Deny'.
how:
1. Ceiling first, before any phone is paired: in happy-config add the iOS default data commands (location.get, contacts.search, calendar.events, reminders.list, photos.latest, motion.activity, motion.pedometer) to gateway.nodes.commands.deny, keep the opt-in commands (camera.snap, camera.clip, screen.record, health.summary, contacts.add, calendar.add, reminders.add) out of gateway.nodes.commands.allow, and set gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false so a paired phone cannot publish tools to agents. Deny always wins and both lists are Gateway-wide, so this can ride in the same config change as MAC-04. The deny list matches exact command names, so unless Talk (VOX-01) is being set up also list talk.ptt.start, talk.ptt.stop, talk.ptt.cancel and talk.ptt.once. 2. Install the App Store app on Tony's iPhone and pair it with a setup code from the Control UI (Nodes, Devices, Pair device) or openclaw qr over the existing Tailscale Serve URL. One code issues a node session and an operator session together; an administrator-minted code approves the device and its first declared command surface in one step, so read the approved command list afterwards and approve any later widening by hand. 3. Access level: Full access carries operator.admin, which is what lets the app review pending exec approvals in general; Limited access drops only operator.admin (write, read and approvals scopes remain) and the docs then promise approval review only for requests that explicitly target that device. 4. Agents: do not grant the built-in nodes tool to any agent (it is owner-only, on the sandbox default deny list, and carries approve and raw invoke actions); if a later feature needs one phone command, use a small in-house plugin tool over api.runtime.nodes.invoke with the node id and command fixed in code. Deny show_widget on

-main, or allow native reports only. 5. Uploads from the app go through the F084 privacy gate, or are switched off with gateway.uploads.enabled: false. iMessage stays the main channel; the app is the surface for long documents, tap approvals and a fallback if imsg breaks after a macOS update. Out of scope for this entry: a second adult's phone. Every setup code carries Gateway-wide operator scopes, OpenClaw says those are not isolation between people, and roadmap section 1b keeps the control plane with Tony while family members only chat. Reopening that is Tony's decision, and it would first need named operator roles (gateway.roles) bound to a verified identity and rehearsed on a test profile, because a Gateway with roles configured refuses operator connections that carry only a device or setup-code token; OCL-03 waits on the same decision.
depends_on: OpenClaw iOS app from the App Store (iOS 18 or later) on Tony's iPhone
Tailscale on the phone (already needed for the Control UI)
happy-config change by Tony before pairing: node command deny list and pluginTools off (same config key as MAC-04)
decision: Full or Limited operator access on Tony's phone
F084 privacy gate extended to app uploads, or uploads switched off
decision (only if a second adult's phone is ever wanted): a verified per-person identity with gateway.roles, proven on a test device first
caveats: Pairing defaults to Full access (operator.admin): the app then also opens Dashboard settings, automations and every agent. Limited access drops only operator.admin; it keeps operator.write, operator.read and operator.approvals, which the docs describe as Gateway-wide, so a Limited phone can still run any agent. Only a role bound to a verified identity narrows that.

With gateway.roles configured, operator connections that authenticate only with device or bootstrap tokens are refused; whether the iPhone app can present a per-person verified identity instead is not confirmed (see unverified).
App Store builds receive push through OpenClaw's hosted relay, a service outside the tailnet; the Gateway stores a relay handle rather than the raw APNs token.
iOS suspends the app in the background: camera and screen node commands need the app in front, and voice is best-effort.
Files a parent uploaded earlier cannot yet be downloaded again from native history; assistant-sent documents are capped at 100 MB.
Progress cards and inline widgets only exist on app and web surfaces, so behaviour will differ between the app and the iMessage thread.
iMessage already covers quick text, and with F001 and F002 it also takes photos and PDFs; the app earns its place only for long multi-page documents, tap approvals and offline queueing.

Turning on gateway.roles changes sign-in for every operator device: connections that authenticate only with device or bootstrap tokens are refused, including a setup-code iPhone and any of Tony's existing token-paired devices. The docs also say roles organise collaboration inside one trust domain and are not a per-person isolation boundary. Rehearse on a test profile before touching the live Gateway.
safety:
The app adds no tool by itself but changes two things. First, uploads reach

-main as files, so the F084 gate and the attachments-to-cloud decision apply to this surface too; gateway.uploads.enabled: false switches client uploads off entirely. Second, runs started from the app advertise inline widgets, so show_widget becomes available unless denied; HTML widgets may load CDN scripts that can see the widget's content, so keep it denied on memory-holding agents. OpenClaw states that session ownership and sidebar visibility are not security boundaries, so keeping the two parents apart must come from roles that limit which agents a profile can run. Outbound messaging and the family-only recipient pin are unchanged.
unverified: The exact command list the current App Store build declares at connect time (the app is not part of the installed package).
Whether a before_agent_run privacy gate (F084) sees files attached from the native app exactly as it sees iMessage attachments.
What the hosted push relay learns beyond a wake request.
Whether sessions started in the app and the iMessage DM for the same parent share one conversation or stay separate under session.dmScope per-channel-peer.
Whether the native iOS app raises a lock-screen alert for a pending approval or question; the docs name wake pushes for the app and approval alerts for Web Push and the macOS app.
Whether a PDF can be sent to the app from another app's share sheet; the docs list the share sheet for images and Files (+ -> File) for documents.
Whether anything can restrict which session a paired phone's own agent.request or voice.transcript events may target; the handler was read and no check was found.
Whether a per-person verified identity (gateway.roles) works with the iPhone app at all; this matters only if a second adult's phone is ever reconsidered.

name: Research agent extra readers: read-only browser behind an action firewall hook, and summarize CLI
description: The research helper can also read public pages that need JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of long articles, videos and podcasts. An in-house hook keeps the browser read-only in code (one profile, no typing, no form filling, no uploads, no page scripts); bot walls and logins stop it.
example: Jordan texts: "What does the rec centre page say about spring swim lessons?" The page shows nothing without JavaScript, so research opens it in the logged-out browser and her own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a 40-minute video and asks for the main points.
how: Two readers, on the research agent only. (1) The `browser` tool on the managed `openclaw` profile, with `headless: true` on that profile and `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Four switches come first: `browser.enabled` (off since M0), the browser tool on research's sandbox tool allow list (it is on the sandbox default deny list), the per-agent tool allow, and a place for the browser to live. First choice is the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked; its image has to be built from a source checkout because the npm install does not include the Dockerfile. The fallback is the host's managed profile through `sandbox.browser.allowHostControl` and an explicit host target, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them. (2) A host stdio MCP that wraps `summarize --extract --json` and returns extracted text from articles, YouTube and podcasts without calling a model; the wrapper pins `--firecrawl off`, holds no third-party keys and checks the address itself. The firewall (formerly WEB-03): an in-house plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`, default-deny and failing closed. It rejects any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned to the agent (a missing profile is filled in or blocked, because an omitted profile means the default one) and rejects `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`. Of the tool's 24 actions it allows only a listed read-only subset (for example status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot). `act` and `upload` are not on that list in this build, which blocks every act kind at once: `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize`, `type`, `fill`, `select` and `click`. If a page later proves unreadable without scrolling, `act` comes back only for kinds on an allowlist of its own (`scrollIntoView`, `hover`), each with an eval case. The hook reads the URL from `targetUrl` first and `url` second, looks inside a nested `request` object, and blocks any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ. Unknown agent, missing field, unknown action or kind, or a parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or times out. Research reads the open web, so there is no site allowlist here; navigation stays http and https under the WEB-01 private-network block. Not built here: the exact-hostname allowlist and the ask-a-parent-before-typing approval branch, whose only consumer is the roadmap's M6 jobs agent.
caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to report them as manual steps, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The sandbox browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. The host alternative needs allowHostControl, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them.

The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. That is why clicks are blocked outright in this read-only build.
A navigation check in a hook sees the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next; the private-network block in WEB-01 is the backstop.
With open and navigate allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the download action ever being called.

The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool schema and can change with any update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook needs a contract test after every OpenClaw update.

summarize runs on the host, outside the SSRF policy that covers web_fetch and the browser, and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks; the wrapper must switch those off and check the address itself.
An independent evaluation on live websites found web agents much less competent than earlier benchmarks suggested, so expect misses on complex pages.
corrections: The catalog says to 'use the host profile'; because research must stay sandboxed, the browser tool defaults to the sandbox browser, and the host profile needs `agents.defaults.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` plus an explicit host target.

The catalog's install line names the tap formula steipete/tap/summarize (as the bundled skill does); the upstream README opened in this run gives `npm install --global @steipete/summarize` or `brew install summarize`.
unverified: `--youtube auto` and the optional Apify token appear in the bundled skill but not on the upstream README; check `summarize --help` after install.
How often rec-portal and store pages block a headless, logged-out browser was not measured.
The hook contract was read, but the browser parameter names come from the tool's schema source and were not observed in a live hook event.
Whether `ctx.agentId` carries the sub-agent's id when research runs as a spawned session; every per-agent rule depends on it.
Whether the hook sees the browser call before the tool applies its own defaults (profile, target), so that 'must be present' can be enforced.
Whether script-rendered pages can be read with the `act` action off (no `wait`, `click` or scrolling); any kind allowed back needs its own eval case.
safety: The research agent holds no private data, no memory and no accounts, and this browser is a managed profile with none of the family's signed-in sessions, so an injected page has nothing to steal. What a real browser adds is a way to act, so the limits on profile, target and actions live in code and fail closed, page script evaluation is off in config, and the home network is out of reach (WEB-01). The hook is in-house code on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it gets its own injection eval cases before the browser is switched on. No profile on this browser ever holds a login, and CAPTCHAs are reported, never solved.

name: Talk mode on Tony's iPhone (native speech loop, operator only)
description: Tony installs the OpenClaw iPhone app and holds a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent: the phone transcribes, the gateway answers as it would a text, and the reply is spoken. The app also adds a Listen action on any reply and a Siri phrase or Action Button shortcut that starts voice. It is Tony's phone only: the app is a full gateway client and a device node, and nothing verified today can hold a second adult's phone to her own agent.
example: Parent presses the Action Button and says: what is on tomorrow, and do I need to pack anything for soccer?
how: The App Store OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone, the same install and pairing as the iPhone app entry (OCL-01), reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Before pairing (limits folded in from VOX-03): the phone command ceiling is in place (device commands denied first; OCL-01, formerly HOM-08); `talk.agentId` is set explicitly and names a memory-less agent, because it is one value for the whole gateway and receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key; `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` stays off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider; and the operator's inspect script gains a read-only listing of paired devices and their scopes. Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for this phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the agent picked in the app (tony-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Other keys: `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button.
depends_on: the OpenClaw iPhone app paired on Tony's phone with device commands denied first (OCL-01; this was IPH-01 and HOM-08)
Tailscale on the phone
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the VOX-04 local engine), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
decision: is a write-scoped gateway credential on Tony's phone acceptable
a written device-revocation step for a lost phone
a second adult's phone only after gateway.roles is proven with the iOS app on a test device
caveats: Audio can leave the house even in the native loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services. The transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.
iOS may suspend background audio, so voice is best-effort unless the app is in the foreground; the Siri shortcut does not bypass unlock or foreground restrictions.
Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup. Talk adds the continuous loop, barge-in and spoken replies, not a new capability.

Everything about the pairing applies here unchanged and is spelled out in the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): the app is a gateway client first, every pairing profile includes operator.read (session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace), `--limited` removes only operator.admin and leaves write, approvals and Talk secrets, the phone registers as a node, App Store builds use a vendor-hosted push relay, and a lost phone has to be revoked on the gateway. On a second adult's phone the other adult's agent memory would be readable.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`). The config repo sets it to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.
There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack: whoever is near the microphone is the user.
safety: Tony's phone only. That is acceptable because section 1b of the roadmap already makes Tony the control-plane owner who can read everything; pair with the limited profile, keep the node surface unapproved, and treat the phone as an admin-adjacent credential. A second adult's phone has no safe placement today: the docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not a boundary between people, and the named-roles feature that could limit her to her own agent rejects the device and bootstrap tokens that QR pairing issues. Voice input is the speaker's own words, so no untrusted-content leg is added to tony-main, and tool policy, hooks and the family-only recipient pin still apply to the agent's tool calls. A child must not use this Talk session: every agent is cloud-backed and Apple Speech on iOS may send audio to Apple.
unverified: Whether Talk still runs on an iPhone paired with a `--voice-node` code. What is certain from the installed scope table is that such a phone loses typed chat and the Listen action (chat.send and tts.speak need the write scope).

Which speech providers pass the Talk-mode check inside `talk.speak`, and whether a local engine set up under tts (VOX-04) can serve as the Talk provider on iOS. The installed code resolves `talk.provider` against the general speech-provider registry with fallback disabled.
Whether a Talk session can continue the same conversation as the person's iMessage thread, or only shares agent memory.
Whether the iOS app can connect its operator session at all once `gateway.roles` is configured.
Whether Tony and Jordan have separate tailnet logins, which a verified Tailscale identity per person would need.
Whether the M0 Tailscale Serve route is owned by OpenClaw (`gateway.tailscale.mode`), which `openclaw qr` requires before it will advertise a tailnet URL.
Whether in-app Talk still works while the phone's node surface is left unapproved.
Whether Talk starts from the inline control on a limited pairing without a first visit to the admin-only Talk settings page, and when exactly the iPhone falls back to its system voice.
